SUN:MART OF THE REPORTS PRESENTED AT THE THIRTY- EIGHTH ANNUAL MEETING, HELD ON 3RD MARCH. 1857. In the ordinary Branch the number of policies issued during the year was 2),567, assuring the sum of £2,715,429, and pro- ducing a New Annual Premium Income of £125,604, The premiums of the year were £396,940, being an increase of £93,665 over the year 1885. Tke claims of the year amounted to £135,341.
The rate of expenditure of the Branch was little more than Ten per cent. of the Premium income. The number of policies in force was 85,089.

An alteration has bs en made in the Regulations of the Com- pany, empowering the Di. ectors in future to pay an interim bonus upon all Participating Policies on their becoming Claims. in respect of any Premiums paid subsequent to the last distribution of profits. The Premiums received during the year in the Industrial Branch were £2,911,295, being an increase of £16,773. The claims of tbe year amounted to £1,123,428. The number of deaths was 135,851. The rate of expenditure of the Branch shows a slight reducion: The number of Policies in force, including 68.099 Free Policies, was 7.111,828. A supplement to this Report will also be suomitted, show- ing how the assets of the Company are invested The tables of the Industrial Branch have been again re- vised, and additional advantages are secured to the Assured which the Directors believe will yet further eohance the popu- larity of the Company. 1314iStA.RY OF THE QUINQI7E7SE4L REPORT. • FOR TEE PERIOD ENDING 31ST DECEMBER, 1886. In the Ordinary Branch the Annual Premium lucerne has Increased from £142.732 to £407,360. The assurance Fund has grown from £744,183 to £1,764,600. In the Industrial Branch the Annual Premium IDCOOIIO has Increased from £2,051,024 to 43.065,551. The Assuransie Fund has grown irom £1,721,493 to £4,937,003. The Total Assets of the Company have grown from £2,580,002 to £6,811.954, being an increase of £4,231,952 in the five years under inspection. The rate of expenditure during the Quinquennium in the Ordinary Branch has remained , nearly stationary, at little more than tee per cent. A reduc- tion of seven and a-half per cent, has been effected in the ex- penses of the Industrial Branch. It will be seen from M. Dewey's Report that the average duration of all the Policies in the Industrial Branch is DOW no less than five and a-halt years, a satisfactory indication of the success which is attending the efforts of the Dirsctors to in- crease the duration of the assurances. EXTRACT imam MB. A. II BAILEY'S REPORT. Having irom time to time been consulted as to the princi- ples upon which the valuations should be made of the out- standing liabilities of your company on the 31st December last, I have now examined the results of those valuations, the pro- cesses employed in obtaining and checking the particu'ars from the records, and the methods adopted to inure accuracy in the calculations. 83M6 notion may be formed of the magnitude of the work when it is stated that the number of assurances In f roe, ex- clusive of annuity grants is 7.196,917; so th .t if each policy were on a different life, which is probably not very far from the truth, the lives of 19 6 per cent, or very nearly one-fifth of the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland, are assured in this company. The business is carried on under two distinct branches, the " Ordinary" and the •s Industrial " In the former, the pre- miums are payable annually, half-yearly, or quarterly; and the terms and conditions resemble those of the majority of the Life Assurance Companies of the country. in the latter branch the rates are higher, because, without exception, the premiums are payable weekly, an arrangement, which the ordinary companies will not adopt on account of the heavy ex- pense and trouble of collection, but which experience seems to show is the only war whereby the wage-earning portion of the community can be reached. For ten years the two B. aeches have been conducted inde- pendently or each other, as if they were distinct societies ; separate accounts being kept, and separate investments made for each. Ileing now, however, oractlcally worked by the same agents.the public select whichever hest suits their con- venience, and conseqently the distinct:loa between the char- acter of the business of the two branches is becoming less. As an instance of this it is noticeable that while the average amount assured by each policy in the s' Ordinary " Branch has diminished since the last Naluation, being now £ll6 against the £137 five years ago ; in the Irdustrial Branch the average amount has slightly increased, and is now £9 3s. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The growth of this Branch has been very remarkaule. The premium income from the assurances is £406,852, having nearly trebled in the qulnquenrium. and being surpassed by only four other Life Assurance Companies In the United Kingdom. The basis upon which the valuation of the liabilities has been made is expiained in Mr. Hughes' report. It may be shortly described as follows —The past ' experience of Assured and Annuitant itves has been adopted for the rates of mortality ; 3 per cent for the rate of Mt- rest ; and 221 per cent of the premium income, which is the whole of what is called the loading, has been reserved for future ex- penses, profits, and contingencies. Of the ample sufficiency of this reserve no doubt can be entertained, especially as it has now been rmolved that the whole expenses of this Branch shall be limited to 10 per cent of the premiJm income. INDUSTRIAL Basricu.—ln this Branch the Premium Income has now reached the enormous total of £3,065,551, pavab e in weekly premiums averaging about twopence each. The ages of the lives assured vary from 1 year to upwards of 100, four- teen centenarians being found open the registers. The females out-number the males in the proportion of 1.075 to 1,000, an excess adnewhat above that of the general population,whereas in the-ordinary Companies the number of male lives assured is found to be about eight times that of the females. A large number of the policies in force have been effected on the lives of children. And, if death occur during the first year of as- surance, the contract provides that, with some exceptions, a deduction shall be made from the sum assured. From these circumstances some modifications in the princi. pies of valuation adopted for the Ordinary Branch become necessary. These are explained by Mr. Dewey in his report, with which I concur. For instance, the table of mortality employed for the Ordinary Branch represents the experience of adult male lives only, children being altogether omitted. For the Industrial Branch, therefore, Farr's English Life tables have been used, and separate valuations m?de for the male and female railis, the mortality of the two sexes being different. Ay sin: the rate of mortality of children, unlike that of adults, diminishes from year to year up to a certain age. And there- foe the risks on lives of children not exceeding ten years of age, and those under all Policies granted during last year, have been treated as short term assurances, for which a nomi- nal iererve only is necessary. With these exceptions, a valua- tion on the same principles as lathe Ordinary Branch has been made of all the outstanding Policies. These facts and figures speak for themselves, and it is hardly necessary to add how eminently satisfactory the results of this I elaborate investigation must be to all who are interested in the welfare of the Company. A WORD FOR THE NAVY. Mrs. Davenport Adam's " Sea, Song and River Rhyme," just liubliahed, is prefaced by a new poem by Mr. Swinburne, entitled. "A Wordlouthe Navy.' In the coterseof the poem there occurs a strong protest against the neglect -of ,naval armaments.. The poet addresses England—

The lords of tty fate, and thy keepers Whose charge is the strene,b of thy shrive', If ttOw they be drearnets and sleepers, • • Or sluggards with lies at their lips, Thy haters and traitrs, False friends or foes descried, Mist scatter and shatter ' _ irt Too soon thy princely pride. iv. • Smooth France, as a servant for rancour, • Dark Muscovy, girded with guile, Lay wait for thee riding at anchor on waters that whisper ar.d smile. They deem thee or dream thee Less living now than dead, Deep sunken and drunken With sleep whence fear has fled.

But thou, though the world shouktmisdoubt thee, Be strong as the seas at thy side; Bind on but thine armour about thee That girds thee with power and with pride. Where Drake stood, where Blake stood, Where fame sees Nelson stand. Stand thou too, and now too Take thou thy fate in hand.

A FRIEND'S HAND IN MINE, LADS. Sometimes 'tie May, lads, The sky soft and bright; We sing on our way lads, With brave hearts and light. But May cannot last, lads; With great clouds rolled, The skies are o'ercast, lads, The world turns cold. A friend's nand in mine, lads, A kind hand and true, In rough ways and dark days— It helps a man through. We've small gifts to give, lads, A poor purse to show, But what man can live, With nought to bestow? A word of brave cheer, lads, A warm.grasp and strong, Beats all your gear, lads, To help hearts along. A friend's hand in mine, lads, A kind hand and true. _

In rough ways and dark days— It helps a man through. Do what you can, lads And do it with might; : God isn't man, lads,/ To judge by the sight. Pence pounds outweigh, lads, When wills are right good, And, oh ! to hear Him say, "He's done what he could." A friend's hand in mine, lads, A kind hand and true, • In rough ways and dark days— It helps a man through. —Frederick Lanqbridge in Leisure Hour for March.

div.head: Tarittits.
div.p: Tarittits.

Fear is a bad habit often formed in childhood and eontinned in a chronic form during life. It is to be cured only or mainly by its opposite—courage. We should choose our friends for what they are, not for what they have, and we should have them always with us—preserved in absence, and even after death, in tete "amber of memory." "He who would eat the kernel must crack the nut— be who would have the gain must take the pain." Right judgment is the kernel of the whole great nut of life, but It is to be gained only by pain and i' diligence, and the determination to know so much of the truth of things as we can get at. A Highlander who had committed a furious assault on a fellow-countryman was apprehended and taken before a magistrate. On being found guilty he was sentenced to pay 10P. Eld., or go to prison for 14 days. He chose the former anemative, and, on paying the fine, laid be- side it another halt-guinea, saying, "She'll pay the same tenean'-seex jeest now over again, for she'll git her twice more when she gets oot." A farmer's daughter during the .rage for albums haneled to Willis Gayllird, an American poet, an old account-book ruled for pounds, shillings, and pence, and requested a contribution. He happily utilised the ' figures as follows:—" This world's a scene as dark as Styx, Where hope is scarce worth 2s. 6d. Our joys are borne so fleeting hence That they are dear at 18d.; And yet to stay here most are willing. Although they may. not have a is. A BUDGET Or TRANSYLVANIAN Forac-tone.—Nine etraws, which must be counted backwards from nine till one, should be placed in a jug of water, drawn from the river with the current, not against; into this are thrown parings of wood from off the cradle, the doorstep, and the four corners of the room in which the child was born, also nine pinches of ashes, likewise Counted backwards. When all these various ingredients have been boiled up together, the water is poured boiling hot into a large basin, and the pot left in it upside down. If the boiling water draws itself into the jug (as of course it will), that is proof positive that the child was bewitched; and the mother should moisten its forehead with the water before fit is cold, and give it (still counting backwards) nine drops to drink. The child that has been bewitched may likewise be held above a red-hot ploughshare on which a glass of wine has been poured; or else a glass of water an which a red-hot horse-shoe has been placed, given to 'drink. In almost every village there used, not lcng ago, to be old women who made a regular trade out of pre- paring the water which was to undo evil spells. The Saxon mother is careful not to leave her child alone until it has been baptised, for fear of the malignant spirits, who may steal it away, leaving an uncouth elf in • its place. Wheeever a child grows up clumsy and heavy, with a large head, wide mouth, stump nose, and crooked legs, the gossips are ready to swear that it has been • changed in the cradle, more especially if it prove awk- ward and slow in learning to speak. To guard against such an accident, it is recommended to mothers obliged to leave their infants alone, to place beneath the pillow I either a prayer-book, a broom, a loaf of bread, or a knife stuck point upwards. Very cruel remedies have some- times been resorted to in order to foice the evil spirits to restore the child they have stolen, and take back their 'SAM Changeling. For instance, the unfortunate little creature suspected of being an elf was placed astride I upe,n a hedge and beaten with a thorny branch till it I 3,7.5 quite bloody ; if was then supposed that the evil I lirdirits brought back the stolen child.—From "Among the Transylvanian Saxons," in Blackwood's Magazine for February 887. THE HYAcrerat TRADE. The hyacinth trade (says a writer in the Standard) is an important branch of horti- cultural commerce. For at least three hundred years it has been cultivated, and as early as 1597 Gerard men- tions six varieties as grown in England. Less than a century later the six had multiplied into many single and double forms, and in the middle of last century the famous Dutch growers of this bloom, "supreme amongst the flowers of spring," offered for sale fifty single- flowered and nearly one hundred double-flowered varieties. One of them, known as "La Heine des Femmes," a single white, is said to have produced from thirty-four to thirty-eight flowers on a spike, and on its first appearance to have sold for more than £4 a bulb: while the "Conqueror," a double blue, brougllt fully, double that price; the "Gloria Mundi" between £2O and £3O, and the "King Solomon" an even higher price. The original of all these plants is not, as many people suppose, the wild hyacinth of our woods, but a scarcely less insignificant Oriental form, bearing on a single spike only a few narrow-lobed "washy blue flowers." The improvements in it are all due to the skill of the gardener, who selects his breeding forms with all the care which the grazier bestows on his Durhatns and Ayrshires. The result is that it is by no means uncom- mon to see spikes of hyacinths six or seven inches long, and thickly set with blooms which measure in circumfer- ence from seven to nine inches. The English nurserymen have, no doubt, done much to bring this plant to what they are pleased to call perfection, though the botanist considers it the acme of monstrosity. But the Dutch growers still maintain their traditional eminence as the champion hyacinth rearers of the world. There is some- thing in the soil of Holland, something also in its humid atmosphere, congenial to these plants, and a great deal in the patient unexcitable character of its excellent people which peculiarly suits them for the placid labour of growing bulbs. Haarlem, which in the height of the tulip mama was the metropolis of this trade, is still pre- eminently the home of the bulb merchants. In a month it will be better worth visiting than at the season when the tourists usually are to be seen in its old-world streets. For in April and the beginning of May the suburbs for miles and miles will be perfectly aglow with the most delicately scented flowers. Whole fields of hyacinths and auriculas, and: tulips and carnations, in the most bewildering variety of colours, impart an indescribable' gaiety to the southern and western sides of the town, and from the conversatidn of the guests at the different hotels it is not difficult to gather that the chief ,business done in the spring is in this pleasing form of merchan- dise. An area of between one and two hundred acres is devoted to hyacinths alone, and the crop is reckoned to he worth more than 00,000 a year to the cultivators of these profitable "crofts." In Covent Garden a single market-grower sells from .60,000 to 70,000 pots under glass, their flowering season being accelerated by forcing, so that from Christmas until the season when they can be grown out of doors hyacinths may always be had by those who choose to pay for the luxury. PRACTICAL DEFINITION.—" What does 'transparent' ! mean?" asked a Scotch Board School teacher lately of his class in the third standard. After a long pause, he ' almost despaired of getting an answer, when suddenly • an urchin with a rough head and dirty face cracked his fingers excitedly. "Well ?" said the teacher encourag- ingly. "My mither, sir." "Your mother! Dear me, hofr so ?" "Because," explained the neglected boy, "when my father cam' hame the ither nicht, he said to my mither, Ha, my leddy, I see through ye noo V" Yoram Tnier BIDS DEFIANCE TO Aosi.—There are some people who turn gray, but do not grow hoary, whose faces are furrowed but not wrinkled, whose hearts are sorely wounded in many places but are not dead. There is a youth that bids defiance to age, and there is a kind- ness which laughs at the world's rough usage. These are they who have returned good for evil, not having learned it as a lesson of righteousness, but because they have no evil in them to return upon others. Whom the gods love die young, and they die young because they never grow old. Two rich old City men, who are very mean and close- fisted, and who put on a great deal of side," met once in the gallery of her Majesty's Opera House. Each was chagrined to be seen by the other in the cheapest part of the house. "What brings 70n Up here?" "To tell the truth, I've got a fearful cold in my head, and, as heat ascends. I came up here where it is warm. Besides, I'm a fearful sufferer from rheumatism. But what brings you up here?" "My opera-glass." "Your opera glass ?" ' Yes ;it enlarges too much. I can't see from the boxes what is going on on the stage. I have to come up here to be able to see at all with it." How HE MANAGED HIS WIFE.—" Blifkins went and married a widow twenty years older than himself, didn't he?" remarked Sam Sample to a fellow-traveller. "Yes —a very extraordinary attachment." "I'm sorry for Blifkins.•=uch marriages never turn out happily. I'll wager she keeps hint in hot water most of the time." "No; on the contrary, she studies his slightest wish.. She was boss for a while, but he found a way to alter that." "How did he do it?" "Why, you see, when- ever she showed an inclination to make things warm, Blifkins would threaten to call her 'ma' in company. He never had to put his threat into execution." CDRIOUS CHINESE PROVERES.—The ripest fruit grows on the roughest wall. It is the small wheels of the car- riage that come in first. The ante who holds the ladder at the bottom is frequently of more service than he who is stationed at the top of it. The turtle, though brought in at the back gate, takes the bead of the table. Better be the cat in a philaathropist's family. than a mutton • pie at a king's banquet. The learned pig don't learn its letters in a day. True merit, like the pearls inside an oyster, is contented to remain quiet till it finds an open- ing. Thq top strawberries are eaten first. He who ' leaves early gets the best hat, and,it ought to be added, umbrella. Pride sleeps in a gilded crown; contentment in a cotton night-cap. . . Hs WANTS No Mons CAMPING OUT.—" No, I don't want any more fishing and camping out," said a swarthy young man in a train "out West." "I tried it once, and I have had about enough to last me a lifetime. My face is one of those that tan pretty badly in the sun, but I didn't realise how badly I had been baked until I had concluded to give up camping out and go to the hotel for the rest of my stay. When dinner was ready, I went in with the other guests, and, the head waiter being pretty busy, I four, d a seat for myself. Imagine my surpiisd and discomfiture when the waiter came rounds ' little later and tapped me on the shoulder, saying, loud ' enough for everybody in the room to hear, 'Beg pandon, sah. but culled pussons not 'lowed to eat at fust table in • dis house.'" . .

JEsTmo.—Harmless mirth is the best remedy against the consumption of the spirits; therefore jesting is not unlawful if it trespasseth not in quantity, quality, or reason. It is good to make a jest, but not to make a trade of jesting. The Earl of Leicester, knowing that Queen Elizabeth was much delighted to see a gentleman dance well, brought the master of a dancing-school to dance before the queen. " Pshaw !" said the Queen, "it is his profession; I will not see him." She liked it not where it was the master quality, but where it attended on other accomplishments. The same we may say of jesting. Jest not with the two-edged sword of God's word. Will nothing please thee to wash thy hands in but the font; Or to drink healths in but the , church chalice? And remember, the whole art is learnt a the first admission, and profane jest will come without calling. It is most dangerous to wit wantonly with the Majesty of God. Wherefore, if even without thine intention, and , against thy will, thou chancest to hit Scripture in ordinary discourse, yet fly to the city of refuge, and pray to God to forgive thee. Sinful jests make fools laugh and wise men frown. Seeing we are civilised English- men, let us not be naked savages in our talk. Scoff not at the natural defects of any, which are not in their power to amend. Oh it is cruelty to beat a cripple with his own crutches! Neither flout any for his profession, if honest, though it be poor and painfuL Mock not a, cobbler for his black thumbs. He that relates another man's wicked jest with delight, adopts it for his own. I Purge them therefore from this poison. If the profane- ness can be scoured from the wit, it is like a lamprey— take out the back, it may make good meat. But if the very staple of the jest be profaneness, then it is a viper, all poison—meddle not with it—Fuller. THE CROCODILE.—In an interesting book, translated from the French, is the following account of the habits of crocodiles :—Hidden amongst the aquatic plants, or squatting in the mud, at other times motionless on the surface of the water, or floating silently, like the trunks of trees, stranded on the mud, or carried on by the cur- rent, they await patiently their prey, or they go to meet itwith their jaws extended, their eyes sweeping the liquid 1 expanse and its muddy shores. One does not see the! slightest motion," says Plumier. "We perceivethat it has changed its place, but in a manner almost imperceptible, j3O quiet are its movements; it might then be taken for a piece of floating wood, and I have many times been so de- ceived." Their colour, their elongated form, their immo- bility, the silence which they keep, deceive their victims. Fish constitutes their ordinary diet, as extras theyoccasion- ally add any of the animals which come to repose on the water, or to quench their thirst on its shores. When the saurian perceives its prey, it dives, and proceeds under the water towards it, and, seizing it by the legs or the muzzle, drags it down to the bottom of the water. To use the words of the missionary just quoted, "The un- suspecting game allows itself to he approached so near that it is snapped up before it has time to spread its wings for flight.' Large cattle are not safe from their voracity. "It very rarely happens," says Livingstonex "that a herd of cows crosses the Liambye without some of the young becoming the prey of the monster." M. du Chaillu witnessed the following scene :—As we were paddling along, I perceived in the distance ahead a beautiful gazelle looking meditatively into the waters of the lagoon, of which from time to time it took a drink. I stood up to get a shot, and we approached with the utmost silence; but just as I raised my gun to tire a crocodile leaped out of the water, and, like a flash, dived bark again 'with the struggling animal in his' powerful jaws. So quickly did the beast take his prey that, though I fired at him, I was too late. Ido not think my bullet hit him ; if it did, it struck- some ,im penetrable part of his mail. Aught seen from 70 to 100 people in each one at the same ti,me. The water could only be changed twice a week, and when 500 or 600 people had bathed in it the water became of a' character and consistency more remarkable than pleasant. He proposed that the extension and improvement of the present baths be a part of the Jubilee programme. Mr. JOLLEY, who seconded the resolution, said that he believed that the unsanitary condition of the baths was the cause of their failure, and the Rev. S. W/LKINSON, who supported it, suggested that Turkish baths should be included. Alderman IlAnnismv con- sidered that this was a work that devolved upon. the Corporation, and Mr. J. E. WRIGHT also thought that it shouldnot be made a Jubilee matter. Alderman HARRISON proposed that the wall in 'front of the Town Hall should be knocked down, the ground arranged in flower beds, garden chairs placed where desirable, and a fountain erected. He believed that there ,would be no more popular method of telebrating the Jubilee.—This proPosal was seconded by the MAYOR, and supported by Mr. BENNETT. Mr. F. A. ROBERTS said that there was nothing fo commendthe scheme to his mind. They should spend their money in things of utility rather than of beauty. Mr. J. E. WRIGHT- supported the proposition, and Mr. 11. ROBERTS opposed it. Mr. FRANcOmn submitted that the Jubilee cele- bration should be in the form of building a Ragged Day School for Warrington. If one could be estab- lished where the poorest children could be partially fed and clothed, it would be conferring a great bles- sing on them. In Liverpool there were-eight or ten such schools. He had nothing to say against other schemes, but if his was thrown over he should go on working for it until he had accomplished it. The Rev. J. F. ROBERTS seconded the motion. Alderman Iltuarsoist•thought the scheme a too gigantic one, and Mr. Jorts WALKER pointed out that in case of the establishment of such a school children who. are novt having their fees paid would, practically, be singled out as paupers. The religious difficulty in teaching would also crop up. Mr. JOLLEY thought, that the proposal was utterly impracticable, and Mr. TWiss remarked that it would deprive the exis- ting ' schools of a number of fees, and a grant for attendance, MT. W. UNSEORTH VMS submitting arguments in favour of the proposal to hold an exhibition in the Drill Hall, when Major BOLTON, replying to a ques- tion by Mr. Birtles, said that on no consideration could the use of the Drill Hall be obtained. The subject then dropped. The CHAIRMAN said that in Warrington the wire trade was nearly beggared by German -competition, and he was afraid it would have a bad time of it;for years to come. Other trades were affected to' some extent. How far a technical school in Warrington would meet the evil he did not know. His experi- ence with the science class was discouraging. Mr. George Crosfield once gave £lOO towards forming a chemical class, and he (the chairman) collected somewhat over .£3OO, and they furnished the pest laboratory that ever was furnished in 'Warrington. The school had since been closed, not for want of funds and of good teachers, but entirely from want of pupils. If a technical school did exist he should be much inclined to say that the, young men in his employ should be compelled to attend it. Mr. T. Mowers and Mr. Twiss supporteid the suggestion, the latter remarking, however, that he did not think there were a sufficient number of educated young people in the town for such a school. The Calm- MAN said the- question was of so much importance manufacturers that they should contribute largely, and Mr. JOHN WALKER mentioned that Blackburn was raising £25,000 for technical schools.' At the first meeting, he said, £6,000 was promised. Warrington, with its multiplicity of trades was, be thought, more in need of a school than most towns.

yet letter came out Sir William Harcourt wrote to Mr. Chamberlain 4, in Ids characteristic style, protesting against such manifestation at a time when they were meeting in amicable council. Mr. Chamber- lain was not loth to reply, and the two right hon. gentlemen have since been going at it hammer and tongs. ' The revulsion of feeling consequent upon the discovery that the sanguine reports alluded to were baseless, has strengthened the ever growing dis- like among Liberals for furtleer proceedings in Conference. Sinee M. Illingwohli hotly expressed the wish that the Round Table was burned,.there has been a notable accession to the section of the party the member for Bradford represents in this view, It is felt that Mr. Gladstone's triumph can- not be long deferred, and there is a natural indis- position to see anything in the way of bargaining with the malcontents. Mahomet, they say, 131118 t come to the mountain, for the mountain will, not advance a foot towards him. I know something,- of the personal views of the gentlemen delekate.d by Mr. Gladstone to.attend the Conference, and, have never found the slightest leaning towards giving up tuiything material to bribe back the Liberal dis- sentients. Of 'course, Mr. Gladstone and: the Liberal party generally would be glad to see the wandering sheekrefurn to,the fold. But their de- sire is not neaely so acute as it is with, the wanderers themselves. Tha disposition, therefore, with Mr. Gladstone and his friends is to "leave tb,em alone," certain that in the end "they will come home and bring their tails behind them.'Whilst the prospects of the Liberal party are brightening, the Government is floundering, deeper in the mire. The stars in their courses fight against Salisbury. He has lost in Sir M. H. Beach, one ot the two members of his ministry who could com- mand the attention of the House of Commons.. The appointment a Mr. Balfour to succeed Sir Michael as Chief Secretary for Ireland marks the hopeless level of mediocrity at his disposal. For this abso- lutely the most arduous and difficult post in the Administration, Lord Salisbury would naturally select the best man at his disposal, and he has selec- ted Mr. Arthur Balfour. For ordinary men the experiences of Mr. and Mrs Gladstone on Thursday night, when attempting to drive home in an open carnage from Victoria-street to Dollis mu, would have suMeed. A. full-blooded young man from the country would shrink' from ,raving the night air in such weather as we have lately enjoyed in London. But on Mont:ay night Mr. Gladstone, dining in Whitehall Gardens, close by the Houses of Parliament, had hiaVictoria wait- ing' and drove home through the bitter east -Wind all the way to Willesden. This would seem on the part of an ordinary man a tempting of Providence. But Mr. Gladstone carries with him, a charm which he holds to be effectual against the mnit vintry Weather. This is a short cape which goes t little way below his shoulders and buttons close round the neck. Wearing this, be believes he could, if he were not otherwise engaged, go and tiadithe North ' Pole. The effect is a little odd. The garment does not appear to have any relations with other pow- I tions of his dress. It seems a relic of an otherwise worn out cloak, picked up in Petticoat-lane. I met him on Monday afternoon walking briskly, down Parliament-street, thus attired. Even had he not been otherwise distinguished, all he met would' naturally turn round to look at this strange figure with the odd-looking tippet. But Mr. Gladstone does not,care for appearances', and thokoughly be- lieves in his tippet, which is; it is said, the sole re- maining relic of the cloak he wrapped ardund him on leaving the House of Commons after making his first speech as Chancellor of the Exchequer. VII. In the morninco only one corpse was found at Sir- Quartre--that of 'Doctor Trifulgas. /twos placed in a coffin, and conveyed with great pomp to Luktrop Ceme- tery, after so: many others the doctor had sent there secundum artans, •

A hard man was DeTrifulgas. He felt so little pity that he only attended those who paid fees in advance. Old Hurzof, eomongrel bull-dog,and spaniel, would have had more feeling than he. Six-Qbatre, inhospitable to the poor, opersed only to thelrich. Moreover, there was a tariff: so much for typhoid fever; so much for conges- tion of:the lisngs, so much for pericarditis, and other diseases, which doctors invent by the dozen, Now Vort • gartif, the fisherman, was a poor fellow, a member of a poverty-stricken family. Why should Dr. Trifulgas have put himself out, and on such a night as thia? ' Why, for knocking me up alone," he grumbled, as he went to bed again, "I ought to have charged ten fret- sets I" _ _

As for old. Hurzof, it is said that, !since that day, he scours the moor, with his lantern relighted, howling like mad. I don't know whether that is so; but so many strange things-happen in that volsinian land, just in the neighbourhood of Luktrop. Once more, I advise you not to look isp 'that town in the map. The best geo- graphers have net yot been able to agree as to its lati- tude or evemits longitude.

Grumbling furiously, the doctor left his bed...andlean- ing out of the window, cried— " Who's thee?" "Vort Kartif's wife." "Fishermant.of Val Karniou?"" . • a Yes; and if you refuse to come he'll die. "Well then,.you'lLbe a widow.' "I've brought twenty fretzers." "Twenty hetzers to go to vita Karniou, feur.ldertses ' from here?" , "Do come !"' . " Be off r And the window closed.

He declared that he 4. would not give way an inch ". on the question of a subsidiary and not a co-ordinate Par. liament in Dublin, or of banding, over the Protestant coun- ties of Ireland to a Dublin Parliament against their will. He accused• Sir 0. 'l'revelyan of "indiscretion" in the re- marks he made at,the Devonshire otmb last week,

To the storm were added, this time, three Imeeks of a more determined character. The doctor was asleep. He awoke; but what a. rage he was in! The window opened, and the hurricane dashed in like grapetslaot. The fisherman—" What,.that wretch again ?" "I'm his-mother." "Bother his mother, and his wife, and his.daughter." "He has had an attack."

Well,,then, let him ,defend himself." "We have received some money," continued the old woman, "on account of the house, which has been sold, to Dontrup. If you don't come, ray granddaughter win lose her father, my drlughter her husband, and I my son." It was terribly piteous to leer the voice of that old. woman. Mk think that the wind was feeezing the very blood in her veins, that the rain was soaking through her lean fksh to the very bones. "An attack equals. two hundred fretzers," r replied heartless Tri f nips. "We have only a hundred and twenty." "Good night, then." And the window" once mere closed.. ' But, on consideration, one hundred and twentyfretzers for. a joUrney of an hour and a half and half an hour's visit would be at the rate of sixty fretzers an hour,. one fretzer a minute: The gain would be small, but was not ' to be despised. Instead of going to bed again, the doctor slipped on his coat, got into his fishing boots, donned his water- proof, put on his sou'wester and mittens. Than, leaving the lamp lighted near his MS., which lay open at page 197, he unfastened the door of Six-Quatre, and paused on the threshold. There 'WS the old woman, 'emaciatedjby four-score years of privation, leaning on her staff. "The hundred-and-twenty fretzers? " "Here's the money, and may God render you a Hun- dred fold!" . The Doctor whistled Hurzof, gave him a small lantern to carry in his mouth, and took the road leading to the sea. The old woman followed, ' •

div.p: . IMITIRIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor Wok his seat at 415 p.m.

HORSE BREEDING. Lord RIBBLESDALE called attention to the breeding and supply of horses. He dilated at some length on the scarcity of half-bred horses, and maintained that with- out an Act Of Parliament for compulsory acquisition, it , 'would be impossible to obtain a sufficient number of horses for war purposes. He was afraid we could net, for even in peace times our requirements were far above our resources. He pointed out that between 186 s and 1872 we had imported 79,131 horses, and • between 1873 and 1882 197,092. Tal.lng these at an average of £55 a head, it showed a loss to this country of nearly £6,000,000. From 1882 to 1886 we had imported 57,432 animals, and during that time • large numbers had also been imported in Ireland. With regard to the length of time it took to obtain foreign supplies, he informed their Lordships that in 1882 it had taken 17 weeks to buy 1,700 horses in foreign markets. Lord HARRIS admitted the importance of the subject, and, having briefly discussed that part of it which re- lated to the supply of horses for military purposes, undertook to consider any scheme that might be sub- mitted to him. The Duke of, CAMBRIDGE did not think the Govern- mentshould undertake the breeding of horses,but thought it would be economical to buy them at two years.oldand keep them in large tracts of.grass land nntil they 'were properly formed. ' Lord WENLOCE thought that every encourageirent should be extended to the farmer in this matter. Lord RIBBLESDALE, in reply, complained that no' re- ference had been made to the Queen's Plates. He did not intend to allow this matter to drop, but would `bring forward a scheme. Lord HARRIS said the question as to the Queen's Plates was a subject for the Chancellor of the Exchequer to deal with, and not for the War Office. The subject then dropped, and their lordships . ad- journed at 5 55 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4 0 p.m. QUESTIONS. Mr. GOSCHEN, in reply to Mr. Mundella, said his -atten- tion had been called to a letter from the Master of Bethel, urging the need of State assistance to local colleges in England and Wales. Be recogilised the im- portance of higher technical and commercial education, but he was not in a position to introduce or facilitate the passing of a measure authorising local authorities to contribute towards the establishment and maintenance of schools and colleges, or to recommend to Parliament annual grants in aid of the same. Mr. Ramis said his attention had been called to the address of sympathy presented to the Secretary of the Post-office from certain officials of the General Post- office, in connection with a difference of opinion between himself and the Secretary, but he regarded it as being Officious rather than official. If he had to take official cognisance of it he wmld certainly consult with the heads of the Government on the matter. • In. reply to Mr. G. W. Balfour, Sir JAMES FEROBSSON said it was reported that some Thibetans had built aefort or gatehouse near the Jelepla Pass, with the view of blocking the road between Thibet and India. Her Ma- jesty's Government entertained no doubt that the Chinese Government would fulfil their engagements in regard to the encouragement of Indian trade 'with Thibet Sif J. GORST informed Dr. Cameron that it was -true • that the heads of dacoits in Bunnah were sometimes brought to headquarters for the purpose of identification by the police, but they were not exposed or carried about the country. The practice had, however, been ordered to be discontinued. SU PPL it. The House then went into Committee of Supplytand - was engaged until a late hour on the Civil Service Sup- plementary Estimates.- On the first vote of £10,860 for • the Science and Art Department, Mr. STUART. Sir H. ROSCOE,: and Sir B. SAMHEISON made some remarks urging•the importance of further provision fcir scientific • and technic education. Sir W. Haar DricE, in answer to criticisms, explained that the additional money required resulted from sail in- crease, due,to the success of the Department, and, adbile admitting the existence of a strong and growing feeling in favour of technical education, pointed out the fiscal difficultyof any substantial extension beyond what as already. provided. Mr. Munner2.4, who made some discursive remarks upon theAubject of freehand drawing, which he desired to see made compulsory in all elementary schools, "bore testimony to the good work being done by the Science and Art Department, and rejoiced that the vote liadibe- • come necessary. After further conversation the vote was agreed to. -• The vote for public education in Ireland, after some discussion," was agreed to; and on the vote for 'the Diplomatic Services, Mr. LAiioncnenz, who objected to the large sums expended in telegrams, moved a reduc- tion of £3,000 spent on this service.—Sir J. Fawn:neon said the-Embassies had been specially warned to .be economical with telegrams, but pointed• out that undue sisarteaing of messages might head to serious remelts; • and on a, division the reduction was negatived by aito to 91. Mr. BRAM...UGH next declaimed against the mission 'of Sir 11. Wolff, which he characterised as altogether ten- aieoessary, and moved the reduction of the vote; and after some discussion, in which Mr. Williamson and Mr. Gourley took.part, Sit J. FERGUSSON, who admitted that the mission of Sir I:1.11701ff had continued longer than had. originally been expected, insisted that the mission • -had done real service, and had laid the foundation of future important reforms in Egypt. 'Mr. Bares justified the action of the late Government sin retaining Sir H. -Wolff, to whose abilities he paid a , %tribute, and, while he thought'his mission might now be • Aletermined, he, was not prepared to hamper the Govern- ', tment at SO critical a time.—Mr. SMITH reiterated his Assurance thatthe mission would not be prolonged un- necessarily, after which the proposed reduction was negatived by 234 to 147, and the vote was subsequently agreed-to. 'The remaining votes of the Supplementary Civil Ser- vice F.stimates,..were agreed to and the Committee' atourneci. MiscEttstmorts.—The County Courts (Expenses) Bill and the first Offenders Bill passed through Committee. The House having resumed, Dr. CAMERON moved the second reading of I the. Licensed Premises (Earlier 'Closing) Scotland SW. He believed the great prepon- derance of -numbers of Seettish members were in favour of earlier closing by an hour.----Colonel anoints moved the adjournment of the debate.—The ad- journment •NVILS negatived.-.-The LORD ADVOCATE thought it would be -better to ascertain what the feeling,was, but it might be left to local option.—Mr. SINCLAIR was. of opinion that when the Government brotsglit in their bill dealing with local government this subjoet .might be included in it.----Lord Cnsicumurn moved the adjournment of the debate.—After a discus- sion adivision was taken, and the adjournment ed the debate ,was carried by 112 votes ag,aiact 100. The Eouse,adjourned at 2 40 a.m. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TVESDAT. The Lewd Chancellor took his seat at 15 p.m. PErrruot.--The Earl of SEL3ORNE presented a pethion in favour.of State-aided colonisation and public worhc. BILL AnvaNcr.n The Truro Ilishopr.c and Chapter Acts Amendment Bill was read a second ‘t:lne. div.head: EX. A.MINER. SATURDAY; MARCTI 12, 1887..
div.p: THE EX. A.MINER. SATURDAY; MARCTI 12, 1887..
THE PROCEDURE RULES. The adjourned debate on the rules of procedure was
resumect.

Mr. HISALY asked whether the Government intended to nake the rules permanent. Mr. W. H. Slum replied in the affirmative. Mr. HFALT said they ought to have proposed to make the rules a standing order of the House. The closure rule as it stood was not a Parliamentary closure, but an anti- Irish closure. • Mr. W. H. Smtrit said it was intended, if the rule were adopted, to propose that it should be made a standing order. Mr. Duzow said the result of the rule would be that those who, like the Irish members, were struggling against oppression and &gr. Ast• the passage of bad bills, would be put down by the Speaker, but the few who happened to be the sons of Dukes or Prime Ministers, and who chanced to form a fourth, or some other party, would be allowed to have their way. (Irish 'cheers.) The rules would inevitably be found absolutely worth- less. The best way to prevent loss of time. and to obviate the necessity of these discussions, would be to do justice to Ireland. (Cheers.) Mr. A. Baani-samin, who was twice called to order by the Speaker for irrelevancy, deprecated the amount of time consumed in these debates.—Mr. W. Janss op- posed the amendment.—Mr. T. P. O'CoNNeR added his protest against the clause.—Mr. Kionsrr (Tyrone) did not believe the rule would be of any service.—Mr. O'Doherty, Mr. Flynn, Mr. John O'Connor (Tippenu7), and Ms. E. Harrington (Kerry) also spoke in opposition to the proposaL The House then divided on the question that the "words of Mr. W. H. Smith's amendment be inserted, namely, a member rising iu his . place may claim to move that the question be now put; and unless it shall appear to the Chair that such motion is an abuse of the rules of the House, or an infringement of the rights of /the minority, the question that the question be now put should be put forthwith and decided without amend- ment or debate.'" The numbers were— For the insertion of the amendment 160 _ _ Against _
make

Mr. PAR;ELL then moved' an amendment by which be proposed to leave out the first part of the rule, the ob- ject-of which he stated was to save the rights of mem- bers in debates on the main question, and the right to move subsequent amendments. As the rule would stand it would be possible, especially in Committee, for a bill to be put through en bloc without the discussion of any of its clauses. The Irish members could not divest their minds of the fact that according to their belief these rules were being passed with the express object of enabling the Government to pass a coercion bill for Ireland. They contended, therefore, that there ought to be some precise form of words inserted in the rule so as to prevent its abuse in the way he had pointed out in domenittee. Me. W. H. Siam said that if the amendment was car- ried, and amendment after amendment could be moved in the way suggested, the rule would be rendered abso- lutely futile. It was inconceivable that any chairman would ever permit such an application Of the rule in committee as would exclude the due discussion of the realand substantial amendments, Rot intended for the purposes of delay or obstruction. He proposed making a standing order of the whole Of the rules as soon as possible after they, were passed. Mr. MOLLOY supported the amendment, and was fol- lowed by Mr. Dmixes, who complained of the way in which the rules proposed to protect the rights of the minority. The Irish members had only won their pre- sent position in the House by making themselves a nuisance. If the rule was passed in its present shape, the Irish members would have no -chance of getting Irish matters attended to, especially in Committee of Supply, when questions which they regarded as vital would not be considered by the rest of the House, and their due discussion would be sure to be stopped by the closure.—Mr. CHANCE and. Mr. O'Colestoß (Donegal) supported the amendment. The debate was continued by Colonel 'Nolan and Mr. - Staveley Hill. .After considerable debate the amendment by Mr. Parnell was negatived by 280 votes to 105. Mr. Smith then propos- leg a merely consequental amendment, it was proposed by Dr. Clarke the debate should be adjourned. The Speaker decided the motion to be an abuse of the rules of the House, and put it to the vote at once, declining absolutely to allow a word from Dr. Clarke or the astenished Parnellites. After the division Dr. Clark explained his object to be to protest against the blocking of bills by a junior Lord of the Treas. wry. The Speaker, amid laughter and cheers, replied that it was precisely because he was aware at this that he had ruled the motion to be an abuse of the rules of the House. The excitement caused by the incident then subsided, but the discussion of the form of closure went on till two o'clock, when the debate was adjourned. The ironworkers of South Staffords.hire have given notice to the employers, through the secretary of the Wages Board, of a demand for an advance of 10 per cent.. on the present rate-of payment.. 'The claim will be con- sidered at the meeting of the board next month.

Two sons of.thelate Mr. Samnel Morley—Mr. Howard and Mr. Charles Morley=havo each presented to the Deaconess Ine...tution and Hospital, Tottenham, the inuni Scent gift or £2,250, in order that the debt of the third wing of tit, hospitd, lately Vat., may at once be removed.

FRIGHTFUL DEATIL-717' ' Carmichael, aged 18 years, was engaged on Sabin 1a.% --lorning in working at a centrifugal sugar-dryi, one at the Roxburg-street Sugar Refinery, Greem.ck, when he fell into the machine, which was revolving at a vgp rapid rate. He was imme- diately thrown violently out again, and on another work- man running to the spot he found that the unfortunate youth was dead. Isaac Whitman, living at Canning Town, London. was arrested OH Saturday on a charge of attempted murder. He was on Friday in a house of ill-fame, and complained of having lost some money. A woman, named Mary Kur- son, endeavoured to turn him out of the house, when he drew a revolver, and fired at her, wounding her in the neck. The woman was removed to the Poplar Hospital, where she lies in a critical condition. Rim' Satvwriesurrs.—As an excited Salvationist meeting, attended by 3,000 persons, was proceeding in the Mechanics'-Hall, Nottingham,-on Sunday night, Mrs. Moore, widow, 52 years of age, suddenly fell back in her seat and expired. The sensation was heightened by the loud screams, of another person seized with a fit, and many women and girls fainted. Major Carter, whose "farewell" caused the demonstration, continued the pro- ceedings, moralising on the event. , Mr. liedgrave, chief inspector of factories, in his report upon the truck system in Scotland, issued on Saturday, recommends that all wages be paid in . current coin of the realm; that deductions from wages for medical attendance and medicine is quite justifiable; that a similar deduction for subscription to a benefit society is an essential advantage to emnlaytis; and that a deduction for materials, tools, gunpowder, and dyna- mite used in works and mines is desirable, if not neces- sary.

INTERVIEW WITH THE OLDHAM MURDERESS.— Mrs. Berry, the Oldham murderess, was visited at Walton Gaol, on Saturday, by Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Minchan, two officials at the Oldham Workhouse. She said to them !—" I have very little hope of a reprieve, and am preparing for the worst, and getting ready for thc end. Ido not say lam ready at the present moment to go with the executioner to the scaffold, but I can say I have no fear of it, and that when the time comes for me to accompany my namesake to the scaffold, I shall be ready to do so. The things of this world are rapidly passing from me, and each friend's face I see for the last time 'is one more ordeal passed through. I look upon the transition from this world as 'stepping into a train from which I shall alight very shortly in a far more beautiful and better place." As she said this the prison clock struck two, and she remarked, "I almost count the hours upon it, and one morning, very shortly, I shall hear it strike seven for the last time, but lam not dismayed, and I hope to have su;fficient strength to bear it. I feel it, as Longfellow dekribes resignation in his beautiful poem of that name." This poem she proceeded to read impressively.

• TILE HORRIBLE WIFE MURDER AT LIVERPOOL.— Emma Downthwaite, the wife of a mariner, living in Rose-vale, Liverpool, had the cleaning and letting of a house in a terrace near where she lived, and last Satur- day week she was about to show a man through the vacant house. when she saw her husband, who had just retxtrned from London, coming home. The husband also saw her, and, coming up, asked, "What business have you in any house with a man?" He was told that she had the letting of the place, and was merely showing a stranger over it, but Downthwaite exclaimed. " You must be after something had," and chased the man away. Be then went home with his wife, being very drunk at the time, and at a later hour locked the street- door, and began an attack on the woman. Having caused her to bleed from the eyes, nose, and ears from the effects of his violence, he caught her by the hair and dragged her to the foot of the stairs,, striking her in the face continually with his fist until she fell. When she was down he' struck her on the bosom about a dozen times, and kicked her violently seven or eight times on the back and aides. He then kicked her on the, ankle and in the stomach. She managed to go tna..tairs to bed, and there he repeatedly struck her again. She co,-ld not see any- thing, her eyes being quite closed. On Sunday toorning she was unable to get out of bed. On Monday, the 28th, he attempted to kick her, and then said, "No, I won't I have given ybu enough already." On Tues- day night she became worse. 'and had a miscarriage, and on Thursday night she died.—k Coroner's jury on Saturday, returned. a verdict of wilful murder against Dowthwaite. He acknowledged ill-using the woman, but said he did not intend to herrn her. ,

LIBERAL CLUB DEBATING SOCIETY, WARRINGTON. Yesterday evening week Mr. Arthur Bennett read a paper to the members of this club on "flow to Federate the Empire and solve the Irish Difficulty." The Rev. B. Filcher presided, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Bennett said that the offer of assist- ance from the colonies to help England in her quar- rels brought the question of federation prominently before the public mind. A further illustration that drove home the necessity for federation was the hold- ing of the Colonial Exhibition in London last year; ' that gave to the public mind an idea of the extent and resources of the Empire that had never been known before. The difficulty with Ireland also brought the matter publicly forward. It had now come to the minds of individuals who were able to dispossess themselves of prejudice, and look at things dispassion- ately, that by the adoption of some federal scheme it would be possible to solve the Irish difficulty. Federation bad two recommendations. One was that it was good in itself as tending to bind the empire together and preserve its unity, and the other was that by the preservation of the unity of the empire, we might manage to solve thd Irish ' difficulty. Before federation could be brought about, some minor steps would of course have to be taken, and it would be a long time before the ultimate result desired could be gained. It had been said that the present Imperial Parliament, which was associated with so many stirring memories,would sink into insignificance if superseded by a new assembly, and that the present Parliament of the Empire would be- come a Parliament of a province. In his plan, which he detailed at considerable length, he did not propose to de- prive the present Parliament of any of its glory, but rather to increase it. He simply asked the Senate to delevate some of the lesser of its daties to subsidiary local bodies. It would still remain an Imperial Parliament, and would be really representative of the Empire. The House of Com- mons would still exist, but would number representatives from the self-governing colonies, and perhaps from India and the Crown Colonies. It was possible that they might be able be cencede to Ireland some scheme of , self-government that would enable her to manage ' her own affairs, and which would also prove beneficial to England, Scotland and Wales, and such home rule might become extended and prove a stepping-stone to Imperial federation. In giving to each of the four parts of the king- dom local self-government they might be guided by the principles adopted in the colonies, and the present Imperial Parliament would be ready for re-arrangement on an impe- rial basis when relieved from purely local matters, and the only remaining task would be the election of colonial re- presentatives. The number of members of the Housemieht be reduced without taking from its capacity for work, and room would thus be made for the colonial members. The advisability of including representatives of the Indian colo- nies would give rise to discussion, but personally he was inclined to favour their immediate admission. His argu- ment rested entirely on the supposed desire of the colonies for a closer union. If the federation did not work well, it need not be continued; its object would be the general welfare, and its sanction the general approval. He thought that federation was a political possibility, infinitely more practicable than any scheme of wholesale disiategration. A discussion followed the reading of the paper, the Chair- man and Messrs. T. Birchall, G. Wallington, S. Barlow, Corney, and T. C. London taking part.

div.head: GENEICAL NEWS.
div.p: GENEICAL NEWS.

The City of Chicago (slarom Liverpool for New York, went ashore at Westhampton on Sunday roorning,got off uninjured, and proceeded to New York. A thick tog set in on Saturday on the Tyne, and along the coasts of Northumberland and Durham. Traffic in Shields Harbour was suspended, and the ferries were stopped, causing great inconvenience to workmen. Mr. Justice Chitty has committed a billiard-marker for three days' imprisonment-for breaking an undertaking given to the court not to engage in the business of a billiardsalG-- within half a mile of his late employer.

Since Guinness converted their business into a limited liability concern, thirteen breweries, great and small, have been put upon the London market, their subscribed capital amounting to nearly twelve millions. A destructive fire occurred on Monday at the mansion of Mr. Morrison, at Gartcosh, seven miles from Glas- gow. Before the engines from the city arrived the house was almost destroyed, but the library was saved. The damage-is estimated at £2,000. Two passenger trains collided, on Saturday, at Laisterdyke station, near Bradford, during a dense fog. The driver was unable to distinguish the signals, and ran into a train standing at the platform. The passengers escaped with a-severe shaking. The men employed at the Pontvmister Tinplate Works, Rises, who have been on strike five months, againsta proposed reduction, resumed work on Monday. There are still ten works standing idle in Monmouthshire owing to the men resisting the reduction.

A WIFE Krum) BY Ecru —DRUNKEN Hosea?rn.—H. Scan- lan, bricklayer, was arrested on Monday by the police at,Coventry charged with causing the death of his wife. The accused returned home in the morning in an intoxi- cated condition, and, it is alleged, assaulted the woman in such a manner that she died a short time afterwards from her injuries.

According to a report just issued from the head-quar- ters of the Salvatlon Army, it appears that during 1886 as many as 148,200 persons in the United Kingdom pro- fessed conversion at the penitent forms of the Army. There were held during the year no fewer than half a million indoor services, and 346,800 open-air meetings in the United Kingdom. ACCIDMITS Ili THIS EIUNTTNG FIELD.—On Monday after- noon Mr. Benjamin Weinman, of Harrogate and Leeds, while hunting with the Bramham Moor Hounds near Welton Station, was thrown from his horse and his neck was broken, death being instantaneous. Deceased was 80 years of age. During the run of the same hounds yesterday Mr. Moorsom, steward to Lord Hare wood, also met with a serious accident.

A dense fog prevailed on the Mersey at Liverpool early on Saturday, causing serions delay to traffic. About noon the Waterford steamer, Nigno/d, landed at the stage the crew and passengers of the African steamer, Angola. The steamers were in collision' early on Saturday,about two miles west of' the bar lightship, with the result that the Angola was sunk, her . crew and passengers being saved.

- On Monday an alarming and destructive fire occurred at Messrs. Aiken and Mausels shipbuilding yard, on the north bank of the river Clyde. A saw mill, a joiner's shop one hundred feet long and three storeys high, were burned. The Patrick and Whitewich fire brigades played on the flames for three hours. The captain of the frre brigade estimates the damage at £l,OOO, and the firm of Aiken and Mausel at £5,000. A person named Osborne, who had been sent to Hollo- way gaol for practising as a solicitor without being duly qualified, brought an action against the 'governor for treating him as a criminal instead of a first-class dernea- nant, and Mr. Justice Denman decided in his favour. The decision was on Saturday reversed by the Court of Appeal, which held that the offence was a criminal one, and not one equivalent to contempt of court.

STRANGE /errant-men MURDER.—At Bury, on Monday, RObert Bannister, butcher, Walkden, an ex-policeman, was committed for trial for shooting, with intent to •murder, Robert Allen, of Radcliffe, on Tuesday last. The prisoner was the worse for drink at Radcliffe, and Allen had promised to find him lodgings for the night. In going through a mill yard where Allen was employed the prisoner fired a revolver at him and shot him in the shoulder. Pormasnoe's Wrms AS DECOITS.—Two married women .were before the magistrates at Macclesfield on Monday, , charged with pretending to tell fortunes. One, who had ibeen.previously convicted, was defended by MT. May, who urged that the complainant had not been deceived or imposed upon. In both cases the fortune tellers had been trapped by policemen's wives, and the magistrates, taking this into consideration, dismissed the cases on .ipayment of costs. Tan KAPUNDA DISASTER.—The second mate of the Ada Melmore—the Belfast barque which was in collision with the Kapunda with such disastrous consequences— arrived at Liverpool on Monday. LYMM LIB ER AL CLUB. SPEECH BY HR.. I. S. LEADA.M.

On Thursday evening week a tea party and enter- tainment were held in the Congregational Schoolroom, Lymrn, under the auspices of the Lymm Liberal Association. At the tea there was a very large number present, there having to be two sittings. Trays were given by the following : —Miss Brevrt- nall, Mrs. Brooks, Miss Brooks, Mrs. E. Brown. Mrs. Bowen, Mrs. Cameron, Mr. G. Clarke, Miss Deville, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. Dutton, Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Grundy, Mrs. Hardie, Mrs. Hodson, Mrs. Holt, Mrs. Kirkland, Mrs. Longshaw, Mr. Lightfoot, Mrs. Loudon, Miss Lowe, Mr. Mackay, Mrs. T. Moston, Mrs. Nighten- gale, Mrs. Robson, Mrs. Ross, Mrs. Swanwick, Mrs. Skifling, Mrs. Thompson, Mrs. Watson, Mr. Wel- ford. Trays were also given by other ladies. After tea the entertainment was given, the schoolroom being crowded. Mr. E Brewtnall presided, and Mr. I. S. Leadam, M.A., Liberal candidate at a previous election in the Altrincham division, was also present. The CHAIIIM&N said that if it were not a fact it might be thought incredible that that was the first Liberal tea meet- ing ever held in Lymm. He was sure, however, that it would have a long succession of others, as the promoters of that meeting had every encouragement to try their bands again, and that very soon. (Applause.) And the atten- dance there that night was not brought together by the drum ecclesiastic or by seductive ladies with yellow brotottets In their button-holes. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Those who had come came from sweet compulsion from within. (Hear, hear.) It was an encouraging fact that that meeting was the outcome of a young organisation in Lymm, the Liberal Cub. That Liberal club was a sterling and honest affair be could tell them for he had had a little experience of it, and it was evidently doing very excellent service. It was spreading and popularising Liberal opinion in Lymm, and he was quite sure that the people of Lymm, like all other people, only had to know something of the truth of Liberalism in order to love it and promote it. (Applause.) Mr. I. S. LEADANt, who was received with marked cordi- ality, directed his prefatory observations to the Primrose League. He said he was afraid that League was a michine employed by the Tory aristocracy to operate upon what he was sorry to call the snobbishness of tne English middle class. (Hear, hear.) To show the contempt with which some of the Primrose people:, looked upon those whom they lured into their toils, he might mention that one of the grand officers of that League wrote a letter to a friend of his, in which she said "We had a most successful Primrose League last night. I enrolled 260 fools." (Laughter.) The only differences which some Conservatives alleged now existed between their party and the Liberals was that the Conservatives were rather the more Liberal of the two. (Laughter.) But there had been one or two opportunities of judging what was the value of Conservative professions. A bill was introduced last autumn by Mr. Parnell, and it was supported by tbe Liberal party, for doing something to mitigate the distress which afflicted the farming and labouring classes in Ireland at the present moment. During the last quarter of the year nearly four thousand persons had been evicted in Ireland for non-payment of rents which the I.iberal party said could not, owing to the fall in the value of agricultural produce, by any possibility be paid. A Conservative Commission, composed of landlords with one exception, had reported that the fall in the value of agri- cultural produce evas so want in Ireland—they estimated It at 181 per cent—that it was impossible to pay the rents fixed more than two years ago. To meet the difficulty arising from that state of things what was called the plan of campaign had been started in Ireland. That bad been defined, and not improperly, as trade-unionism applied to agriculture. The plan of campaign was represented as a combination against the payment of all rent. It was no- thing of the sort. It was a combination against the pay- ment of rents such as a Tory Commission declare the far- mers were unable to pay. Now the object of the coercive measure which had been announced by the Government was the suppression of the plan of campaign. Ha (Mr. Leadam) was very much pleased to see that Sir William Cunliffe Brooks had expressed his antipathy to coercive legislation for Ireland, but that gentleman did not appear to have re- membered that there was an allusion to a coercive measure in the Queen's Speech. (Hear, hear.) It was alleged that the Conservative party were ready to treat the Irish just as they treated the English. Was that so? There was a plan of campaign started some four or five years ago in the counties of Kent and Sussex against the payment of ex- traordinary tittle. The farmers in those counties admitted that the extraordinary tithe was legally due, and that they were able to pay it. But they combined together to resiet payment of it. What happened ? Why as a result of that combintOion they got a bill passed through Parliament which abolished extraotdinary tithe altogether. (Applause.) What did the Conservative Gov- ernment de when they found themselves confronted by a plan of campaign amongst the farmers of Rent and Sussex? Did they arrest the president and secretary and put them in gaol it No, Kent and Swages returned none but Conserva- tive members to the House of Commons, and if a Conserva- tive Government had dealt in the some way with the plan of campaign in those two counties that they now desired to do in the case of Ireland there would not have been a Con- servative member left to represent those two counties. (Ap- Platlee.) What was sauce for the goose was sauce for the gander; therefore the plan of campaign was not necessarily a heinous offence and a crime on the other side of the Chan- nel. What was the object of the Conservative Government In endeavouring to suppress the plan of campaign? It was to maintain rents at their nominal value, and then make the English taxpayer make up the difference between the nominal value and the real letting value of the land. The Conservative party 11.4c1 one paramount interest which ran through the whole of Its policy, and that was the in- terest of the landlords. It WRS emphatically a landlords' party, and its attention was devoted chiefly to the rights of property. Liberals, on the other hand, thought more of the rights of their fellow;oeings, and looked at the rights of property only as seen through the rights of men. (Ap- platiss, I Afterwards an excellent programme of songs. recitations, to., was rendered by D. Barr, Miss Riley, Mr. Furness, Mr. W. H. Wallington, Miss Schub, and Miss Bird, and the proceedings were brought t) a close by the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 12, 18817.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 12, 18817.

LORD SALISBURY was once described by Prince BISMARCK as "a lath painted to look like iron ; " and the more we know of our PRIME MINISTER the more we appreciate the force of the observation. He is very brave in talking about what should be done; but very timid when the time comes for action. Whenl Mr. GrAnsToNE was in power, no one was , louder than Lord SALISBURY in preaching the necessity of "resolute government "in deal- ing with Ireland; but now that he is in office it is obvious to everybody that he holds the reins with a feeble and fumbling hand. The Liberal Unionists counted upon his doing something when they gave him the chance; and they are now in despair at finding that he cannot get beyond talking about the diffi- culties of the situation. That he can do to perfection; he is a splendid talker. Speaking at the inaugural dinner of the National Con- servative Club, held in London on Saturday evening, he said: —" This Irish question, as we look at it now, seems to us like an evil dream. It is one of those nightmares where a danger or a horror presses upon you which you feel that you ought to be able to dissi- pate, but something fetters your limbs and paralyses your energies, and you are unable to make the necessary movement by which the danger or the horror can be dissipated." This is a capital statement of the case so far as the Government are concerned—it could not, in fact, be better put—but what a confession of hopeless impotence! Following, as it does, so soon upon the talk of twenty years of reso- lute government, it is calculated to make Lord SALISBURY the scorn alike of gods .and men. The present critical state of things is, he continues, 'disgraceful to law, disgraceful to constitutional government;" and most people will add especially disgraceful to the party which calls itself the Con- stitutional party. Lord SALISBURY does not, of course, admit this; it is the law which is at fault, and he wishes it to be remem- bered that the Nlinistry are " bound to walk strictly within the limits of the law." Pre- cisely ; but Lord SALISBURY forgets, or, per- haps we should say, coolly ignores, the fact that it is entirely owing to the bungling of himself and his colleagues that he is not pos- sessed of some of the legal powers for which he ' is now clamouring. He deals with people as if they had short memories, but they must have had no memory at all to forget that the Tories themselves allowed the Crimes Act to lapse when they came into office in 1885— and that, too, in the very teeth of the most solemn warnings of their predecessors. Is it fair—is its decent of him—to complain that a weapen is not to his hand which he has de- liberately thrown away? Lord SPENCER pre- dicted that as a coßsequence of the Tory party setting aside the Crimes Act, in order to secure the Irish vote, it would be found impossible for the future to rely on coercion as a policy, and this prophecy would seem to be close upon fulfilment. Lord SALISBURY confesses his incapacity to govern as the law stands; and he will find that coercion will fail him if the law should be altered. "The whole machine," he says. " works well, ex- cept one essential wheel ;" and his idea of rectification is that " the wheel must be either refitted or dispensed • with." The PRIME MINISTER would seem to have a taste for similes taken from me- chanics, but he is not always happy in their application. It will strike most engin- eers as ludicrously absurd to suggest that a machine which does not work well may be set right by dispensing with an "essential wheel." Perhaps his lordship, if he had a watch which, like the celebrated donkey, "would not go," he Would endeavour to make it move by leaving out the mainspring. The wheel— to revert to the simile—which he would set aside is trial by jury in Ireland. Notwith- standing the shameful jury-packing to which the Government have resorted in Ireland, it has happened now and again that somebody of the wrong colour has got into the box and spoilt the verdict of which they were so cock-sure. Lord SALISBURY would therefore do away with juries; but it remains to be seen whether Parliament will soil:lmq this nefarious attempt to strangle the liberties of the people of Ireland. He proposes a remedy which is no remedy at all ; it is a remedy which will intensify the disease. The social condition of Ireland is not to be im- proved by robbing the people of freedom, but giving them more. We need to set aside not trial by jury, but, to borrow a phrase from Lord BEacoNsFrErao, that " orginised hypocrisy—a Conservative Government."

The Welsh have been celebrating St. David's Thy, at Earlestown, by fraternising and nationalising. There is something in what Mr. H. Richard, M.P , says about their being, as a rule, "backward in -coming for- ward." But they will alter all that now that they have set themselves the task of disestab- lishing the English Church in Wales.

It is a pity that the chief draughtsman at Chatham Dockyard has not been subjected to a more severe punishment than dismissal from the service for betraying his trust by fur- nishing -confidential information to certain Foreign Powers A taste of " the cat" and a packing off to the tune of "The Rogue's march " would not have been to much for him.
