Bradford at the last election returned a Tory member—the first Tory since 1865— and the Government, in their gratitude, are making six Tory magistrates, The Town Council, having an eye to the fact that the Liberals when in office were not out-and- out in their nominations for magistrates, have expressed their disapproval. But what of that? TheConsetvatives act on the adage of "The spoils to the victors"; and with them it is natural to ask—what is the use of being a wire-puller if you cannot become a magis- trate ?

Sir George Trevelyan recognises that the game of governing Ireland is up so far as the Tories are concerned ; and he is anxious now that the Liberal party should again become a united party. He accepts the inevitable, and thinks the agony has been sufficiently prolonged. Not so with Mr. Chamberlain; he, of course, knows that the Tories will not settle anything ; but wants to make terms before returning to the Liberal camp. He has a right to do so, and Gladstonian Liberals have an equal right to reject his offer if they do not like it.

has lived in both districts—for no less than a quarter of a century in each—and, as his ear and pen have been constantly at work. he has been enabled to bring unrivalled knowledge to the task he has set himself. The most casual observer who has been in the habit of going from one part of Lanca- shire to another will have noticed great dif- ferences in the use of the dialect; but there are few who will not be surprised to learn, on the authority of Mr. CUNLIFFE, that there are two pretty distinct dialects within the parish of Rochdale. Rooley Moor is the dividing line. " On the northern, or Rossen- dale side, from Bacup to Edenfield, the Rossendale twang.' as the local dialect is called, prevails in its full strength ; while nowhere in the valley of the Roche—on the southern side—is the patois which gives im- mortality to the writings of TIM BOBBIN, more racy than it is on the cloughs and hamlets on the slopes of Rooley Moor." A difference—but not so great—is noticeable between the dialects of Blackburn and Dar- wen, which are only four miles apart. The twang of the latter is much broader; and it may, indeed, be laid down as a rule that the smaller the place, and the nearer it is to moorland, the broader will be its dialect. The cane of the schoolmaster and the fric- tion of large towns are doing much towards ridding us of the dialect, and there is all the more need, therefore, of such a scandard Glossary as the one Mr. CUNLIFFE has pre- pared. It is desirable, of course, that the children in our schools throughout Lanca shire should be able to speak pure English ; but it does not by any means follow that they should be taught to despise the dialect as something barbarous. Where is the Scotchman, however learned or refined. who is not proud of the songs and poems of BURNS, the best of which are unquestion- ably written in the dialect? And shall Lan- cashire men have no regard for the diamonds, rough though they be, of TIM BOBBIN, of BEN BRIERLEY, and Of EDWIN WAUGH? Wit and humour, and good sense and good feel- ing. must be welcomed everywhere, with open arms, whatever be the mode of their expres- sion. And, then, what force there is in some of our dialect words! As EMERSON some- where has it : Scoff of yeoman, strong and stark, . Goes like bullet to its mark. Take the word " backset ;" how expressive it is of giving support financially. There is the word " thrutch," too; push is altogether weak Eompared with it. We have been look- ing through the Glossary with a copy of " Waugh's Lancashire songs" beside us. and have noted a few apt instances of the use of remarkable words, which, as they have in- terested us, may interest our readers. " Ballis- pipe " means the windpipe, and WAUGH uses the word effectively in " Owd Pinder " : "Go, sell my rags an' sell my shoon; Aw's never live to trail 'em; My ballis-pipes are eawt o' tune, An' th' wynt begins to fail 'em." Toppin " is described by Mr. CUNLIFFE as "the hair on the forehead ; "it has no equiva- lent in ordinary English. " Toppin" is also used, we may add, in some parts of Lanca- shire as meaning first rate ; for instance, "a toppin dinner," or "a toppin singer." WArTorr uses the word in the first sense, thus : "So, aw'll talk very prettily to her, as heaw, Or else hoo'll have houd o' my toppin PO' neaw." The word " liefer " is given as meaning " sooner ; more willingly ;" but it conveys some,hing more than this, as in the following case : "An' some are so quare i' their natur That nought wi' their stomachs agree; But he that would liefer drink wayter, Shall never be stinted by me." The Glossary gives the word "hutch" as I meaning "to lie close, followed by ' up' ; hutch up." This is striztly correct; but what a world of additional force it gains when, with a stroke of genius, WAUGH employs It in this connection:—

_ Aw peeped into my cot last neet ; It made me hutchin fain; A bonny fire were winkin breet I' every window pane; Aw marlocked upo' th' white hearthstone, An drummed o' th' kettle lid, An sung "My neest is snug and sweet, Aw'llgo and fotch my brid !" As an instance among many of the difference in speech between the two districts which the Glossary covers, we may mention the word "toll, a tax"; iii Rochdale the dialect word is "tow," and in Rossendale and other parts of East Lancashire it is " towl." WAUGH uses the first form— "An when aw come to dee, An death has ta'en his tow, Aw hope to leet o' thee— God bless thi snowy pow!" Mr. CUNIAFFE, it should be stated, aims at giving literary form to the dialect; but he is quite a purist as to its use. He has no sympathy with those who spoil the dialect by trying to write it so that it will he under- stood by everybody. He says "if the dia- lect is to be preserved, they must show their regard for it by writing less like those who don't care for it, and more like authors who understand it." He would have the native Doric presented in every case as it is spoken ,by natives : and finds fault with WAUGH for failing in one of his tales to keep a dis- tinction between the dialects of R ossendale and Rochdale. Into these matters we cannot go for , lack alike of knowledge and of space; but we can confidently say that there is every evi- dence in the Glossary that the ,compiler thoroughly understands his work, and that he has done it remarkably well.

It was attended by Mr. Thomas Kill, sur- geon, who found that it had not been seriously hurt. LIVERPOOL, MANcuzsran, and District Loan and Discount Company. Eariestown branch, 7, Wellington- street, Eariestown. Established 1882. Applications .can be made, daily.—Advt. ROBBERY OF CA,NDLESTICES.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. W. Blinkhorn, John Beddard, a young man, residing at 8, Manley- street, 'Warrington, was charged with stealing three brass candlesticks, valued at is 6d, the property of Mrs Mary Brimelow, landlady of the Clock Face ' Inn, Bold, on Saturday night. Superintendent Johnson stated that the prisoner was one of a num- -1 ber of young men who visited St. Helens on Satur- day afternoon on the occasion of the football match between St. Helens and Warrington. Mary Brime- low, prosecutrix, deposed that about eight o'clock on Saturday night a lot of men called at her house on their way to Warrington, and she afterwards missed the candlesticks. Christopher Tomlinson, a young man, said he was driving with others in an omnibus to Warrington, and they stopped at the , Clock Face Inn. Witness saw the prisoner put one ' of the candlesticks in his pocket and he afterwards told the driver of the 'bus. John Walton, conductor of the omnibus, stated that. just as they were leav- ing the Clock Face Inn the prosecutrix came to the door and shouted—" You are a lot of Warrington thieves, you have stolen my candlesticks." Witness had the prisoner pointed out to him by the last -Wit- ness, and the three candlesticks produced were found in the prisoner's possession. Information was given to the police and the prisoner was appre- hended. The prisoner was remanded until next Monday, and was admitted to bail.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—Misa Emma Kirkham, of Albert-street, Ituncern, has been appointed essistant mistress in the mixed department of Greenway-ro ret Board school. NEW CURATES FOR RUNC,N3N.—The Bishop of Chester (Dr. Stub* held an ordin trim on Sunday at Chester Cathedral, when the Rev. James Duncan Oz acne, 8.A., of St. Edmund Hall, Oxford, was • rdaine I aeacen and licensed ti All Saints', It incorn. George 14 isher, B A., of Bishop Hettield'e Hall, Durham, was also ordained deacon and licensed to Holy Ti laity, Etuncern. MR. J BRUNDRIT, J.P. RUNCORN.--AI the dinner of the Altcer Coursing Club, held at the Adelphi Hotel, Liverpool, on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., of Runcorn, occupied the vice-chair, Mr. Harold Brocklebaok presiding. Coursing commenced on the following day, and Mr. Brundrit'e Bop, entered for the S,pliton Stakes, was put out in the first round by Mr. Bibby's Bleckmore. Mr. R. W. Abbot's Aurtfer, which was Mr. Brundrit's nomina- tion for the Waterloo Cup, divided the Croateth Stakes with Mr. G. Robinson's Raphin. • SUDDEN DEATH AT FARNWORTH. Mrs Mary Ducker, aged 59 years, a widow, who carried on the business of a grocer and provision dealer at Church-street, Farnworth, died very seddenly early on Tuesday morning. Mrs Ducker awakened her servant about five o'clock, and com- plained to her of being unwell. Medical aid was immedi- ately summoned, but she died about ten minutes after the arrival of Dr. O'Neil. Death is supposed to have been caused by fatty degeneration of the heart, for which the de- ceased had been previously treated. RUNCORN WOMEN'S JUBILEE OFFERING.—A meeting summomd by Lady Brooke, and presided over by her lady- ship, has been held at Runcorn, with regard to the women's Jubilee offering to the Queen. Lady Broke informed the ladies present that she had been asked by the Duchess of Westminster to look after the Runcorn district, and she hoped every street would be visited by the collectors. Any sum would he received from one penny to a pound. Collect- l ing nerds were distrilented, and districts were allotted to the ' ladies present. BRUNSWICK I3SPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.— A debate on" smoking "took place under the aaspicee of this society I on Wednesday evening. It was initiated by Mr. Clegg I , who read a deer end argumentative paper on" Must we put his pipe out ?" The essayist was happy in the selection of the humorous anecdotes with which his paper was inter- spersed, and answered his question by an emphatic nega- tive. Messrs. J. D. Jones and Pooale opposed the paper, and argued that smoking was a public nuisance and that its physiological influence was buaeful. Mr. W. Millington followed in support of the essayist, to whom a vote of thanks was warmly accorded. PROPERTY SALE A.T WIDNES —OR TOursday evening, at the Central Hotel, Mr. B. Dutton offered for sale by public auction a lot of property occupied by Mr. Imieon, which consisted of pawnbroker's shots, barber's shop, end private house, together with six dwelling-houses adjoining. The bid- ding began at £7OO. and rapidly rose to £L,OOO, when th ere was a pause. Finally, the lot was knocked dawn to Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. for £1,105. The auctioneer passed rapidly through the other lots without obtaining a bid Leigh enough to reach the reserve, which in most cases were very low. It is certain many of the lots will be sold privately, as the whole of the property is well situated. Messrs. Robert Davies, Sharp. and Kitkconnel were the solicitors for the vendors. POOLE'S MYRIORAMA AT RUNCORN.—This excellent en- tertainment has been patronised by good audiences at Run- corn Public Hall during the past week. Exciting events both on sea and land are admirably depicted, the realism of the scenes being enhanced by skilful dioramic effects. The pictures of the recent Egyptian war and the Nile expedi- tion, concluding with the march past of the victorious troops before the Queen, were probably the most interesting. An enjoyable change was provided by the songs of Mr. Harry Stewart, whose astonishingly rapid transition from character to character called forth unstinted applause. Mr. Felix Somers produces much mirth by his clever ven- triloquial performance, and the "natural magic" of Mons. de Veye, who also undertakes the duty of guide, was greatly appreciated. A JURYMAN'S QUALIFICATION AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an iaquest at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, on the body of an infant throe weeks old, daughter of James Bennett, a chemical labourer, of 33, Nelson-street. Mr. Singleton, butcher, Victoria-road, objected to being on the jury because he was not a rate- payer. The Deputy Coroner said the only question for him to decide was whether Mr. Singleton lived in Lancashire, and secondly whether he was an intelligent person. In the first place he knew that Mr. Singleton lived in Lancashire, and he had the appearance of being an intelligent person. Mr. Singleton, therefore, had to serve. It appeared that on Sunday night Bennett, his wife, and three children slept in one bed, and next morning the infant was dead. A verdict to the effect that death resulted from being over-

lain was returned. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery on Wednesday. Mr. W, H. Rogerson presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Whittaker, G. Moss, H. Coleburn, and W. F. Salkeld (clerk). It was re- ported that during the eleven months ending February 25 there were 300 interments, a decrease of 13 on the cor- responding period of the previous year. The fees received daring the 10 months ended the same date amounted to £298 28 23, decrease £7 12 Bd. The report of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Moss. stated that the receipts for the month amounted to £2B 12s, and after paying wages, &c., the balance of £l7 78 was paid into the bank. It was recommended that p-ecepts be served upon the overseers for £lOO on account of current expenses, and for ZOO on account of sinking fund. Interest of £BO on mortgages was recommended for payment. It was resolved to ask the overseers to call a meeting of the vestry to ape point anditors to audit the accounts of the Board. CONCERT AT ZION SCHOOL, WIDNES —A concert in aid of the funds of the Free Church School, Oakland-street, was held on. Monday evening. There was a good audience, and the Rev E. Hall, the pastor, occupied the chair. The choir was responsible for all the musical items of an inter- esting programme. and sang several choruses and r tri songs in cepital style, under the leadership of Mr J. Betney, Mrs Lock sang the solo "Violete;" the trio, "We've gained the silvery waterside," was given by Mrs Lock, Miss F. Causey. and Mr J. Betney; quarter, "What is thy song, sweet bird of night," Mrs Lock, Miss Causey, and Messrs Edward Evans and John Betney; duet, "Voice of the wild waves," Mrs Joseph Betney and Mrs Wilcock ; solo and chorus, "Now, who will volunteer." Mr Edward Evans (encored). Mr. Betney gave a reading entitled "The Bash- ful man," and recitations were given by Miss E. J. Betney, Mr Greig. and Mr A. Smith, the contribution of the last- named being in the Lancashire dialect. Mr. A. Ogden ably officiated as the accompanist. FUNERAL OF MISS JOHNSON AT RUNCORN.—The isle - ment of the body of the late Mies Jane Johnson, of iii.z.ber Runcorn, whose death occurred on the previous Friday.to k place on Wednesday mornitig at the Runcorn Parish Church. The deceased lady, who had attained the age or 80 years, was most generous in her benefactions to the poor. and she was an ardent supporter of Holy Triniiy Church and day schools. She was the sister of the 140 Messrs John and Thomas Johnson, the founders of the chemical trade in Runcorn. Those present at the funerel were Mr J. Alcock Johnson, Mr Ernest Johnson, Dr C•rruthers, rr Mc- Dougall, Mr W. Haves, Mr Sharp (Warriagton), and Mr. James Biggins. The body was met at the church by Dr Robinson, Mr J. Brundrit, J.P., and Mr W. Whittaker. The Rev W. Preston conducted the burial service, the lesson in church being read by the Rev A. Maitland Wood, vicar. The coffin, which was of polished oak with brass mountings, was made by Mr James Dutton. Mr W. H. Rogerson acted as undertaker, and Messrs Yarwood and Son supplied the hearse and mourning coaches. ALLEGED FRAUD ON THE RAILWAY AT RUNCORN.—Ai Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, W. J. Shore, ship owner, Runcorn was summoned to appekr before Mr. Chas. Reynolds and 'Mr. James Handley, to answer a charge of 'having, on the 17th February, travelled from Roue irn to Edge Hill without previously paying his fare, and with In- tent to avoid payment The defendant did not appear.— Mr. Emend, who represented the London and North- Western Railway Company, said be expected an application' for an adjournment to be made that morning on the defen- dant's behalf. The defendant appeared to think that every- body ought to give way to him. On Saturday morning he admitted the offence $o him (Mr. Ferrand). and said he should send some one to plead guilty for him, and asked him (Mr. Ferrand) to deal lightly with the ease.—Mr. A. Light- burn explained that the defendant had to meet the official receiver in bankruptcy that morning, and therefore could not be present —Tee Bench declined to hear the case in the defendant's absence, as they were both interested in his affairs, and after some conversation it was decided to adjourn the case for a week. NEWS FROM A RUNCORN YOUNG MIN IN AESTRALIA.—A young man who left Runcorn some years ago to gettle in Adelaide, Australia, has just written a letter to a friend in Runcorn in which he gives an account of his fortunes in his new sphere. The writer contrasts the public schools of Australia with those of the mother country, and regrets that his native town is 80 far behind in matters of education. He then goes on to say "To-morrow is Christmas Day (110 in the shade). I am organizing a shooting and fishing party for a ten days' camping out expedition en the Coo- rong. We expect to have fine times, away from civiliza- tion, shooting our own food and cooking it. The weathel• will be so warm that we shall only need our shirts and hats. 11bave just finished another trip in the interior— I suppose about 1,500 miles—and have profited by it. I hold 100 &bares in a good silver mine, and may make a fortnne out of them. These may be castles in the air, but if they turn I, out as I expect, I will show my gratitucTh and my love for my native town of Runcorn by sending a small sum as a nucleus for a better scheme, or offer a scholarship which may give the Runcorn lads some ambition above that of becoming labourers in a soap factory."

Various rumours are in the air as to the attitude of Lord Hartinaton ; but the most probable one is that he will want to try coer- cion before listening to anything in the shape of Home Rule. He has a stiff upper lip, and doesn't know when he is beaten. The Burn- ley election must have been a bitter pill for him to swallow; but he can swallow bitter pills, and without making much of a face either. It is, perhaps, as well that he should back Lord Salisbin y up until things get as bad as bad can be. The longer the spell of Tory ism, the greater the reaction.

Sir Henry Drummond Wolff is receiving £lO 000 a year for doing "just nothin7 at all" in Egypt. And he keeps on doing it. Sir Henry has made up his mind that he will hold out as long as the money lasts. He didn't serve Lord Randolph for nothing, and he is having his reward. It was very considerate, of course, for his lordship to provide for his henchman; but it would lave looked better if he had done it at his own, and not at the public, expense—particularly as he has set his face against extravagance in national expen- diture.

The strike in New York is said to have cost nearly one million sterling, and the strikers are asked to ponder over the amount, and admit what fools they have been. But there is another side to the question. We never heat anything of estimates as to the amount saved by wages being kept up through fear of a strike. Strikes are generally the outcome of acts of folly on the part of masters as well as men. When the relations between em- ployer and employed are controlled with wis- dom, a strike will .be the exception, and arbi- tration the rule.

Four men were injured at Bold Colliery, and Mr. Jackson, the manager, like a humane person, sent for a doctor. The Company, it seems, were not liable, the injured men being in the employ of a sub-contractor. And so Mr. Jackson was sued personally for Li+ I2S for surgical and medical attendance. The case is one which ought never to have come into court ; and' we are not surprised that, as the doctor refused to accept £to in settlement, the Judge gave an order for something less, A doctor is, of course, en- titled'to be paid for his services ; but he ought to be tender towards a man who has accidentally fallen into one of the pitfalls of the law.

. --- Those who are advocating the freeing of Warrington Library are too wide awake to fall into the trap which is being set for them when it is suggested that they must go in for an Act to increase the library rate. They believe that wbat man has done man can do ; and, as there are scores of towns in the kingdom that are maintaining a " free" library out of a penny rate, they are justified in insisting that an attempt shall be made to do the same in Warrington. They do not see why as much should not be had for a penny in one town as another. . The idea that it is pauperising to urge that the library shall be made " free " is a compound of ignorance and impudence. The humblest inhabitant who pays his rates is on I a level in this respect with the Mayor him- self. He has complied with the law, and that is all that can be asked of him. To say that he must pay again before he can have the full use of that which is provided uncle': the law is a piece of imposition which ought to be resisted, whether the matter in- volved be a penny or a pound. The Public Libraries' Act does not provide that a citizen • shall be taxed twice for the same thing.

A ST. HELENS DROWNING CASE.—The dead body of John Banks, middle-aged, an ex-ticket collector at the St. Helens Station of the London and North- Western Railway, was found in the St. Helens Canal, near Parr Mill, on Friday morning. Deceased, who had been in the army and had served in India, was at a trotting match in Parr the previous after- noon, and afterwards called at the Black Horse Inn. Ho Qv he got into the canal is a mystery. SIR GILBERT GREENALL'S JUBILEE GIFT.—It is stated that, although the various amounts have not yet been definitely decided upon, Sir Gilbert Greenall.s Jubilee gift of £5,000, to be devoted to church accommodation in Warrington, will pro- bably be distributed as follows ;—New church for St. Peter's district, £1,500; new church for Ather- ton's-quay, £1,500; renovation of Trinity Church, £2.50; Mission-house for St. Paul's-Church in Hoyle- street, .E7so;' Mission in Bank-street for the Parish Church, £750; Et. Barnabas' Church School, £lOO. • Public Analysts have submitted CADTWEY'S COCOA 40 close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining aad nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— dvt.

Rearms Al NORTON.—On Thursday a strange dog was discovered on the estate of Sir Richard Brooke, and as the animal was suffering from rabies it was shot by order of Mr. Evans, the agent. - WIDNES POLICE COURT—At this court on Monday, Thomas Winr, John Walker, Sarah Jervis, John Taylor, and Emma Smith, were each fined for drunkenness.—Ellen Knockton, for being disorderly, was committed to gaol for seven days. TREF: BY A litteconst WOMAN. At the Northwich Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Margaret Bramwell, of Run- corn, and Mary Reilley, of Widnes, were each sentenced to two months' imprisonment for stealing £2 103 from the person of James Davies, a boatman, of Middlewicb, on Friday night. ASSAULT ON A POLICE-SERGEANT AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions. on Monday, Emily Travers, a young woman with a baby in her arms, was charged with assault- ing P.S. Blair whilst in the execution of his daty.—On Satur- day night the sergeant arrested a man named Kennedy on a warrant, and the prisoner followed them along Church- street, making rise of filthy and threatening language. She concluded by striking the officer on the face with his fist.— A fine of 5i and cosis, Os 4d, was imposed. j CAMBRIDGE LOCIAL EXAMINATIONS.—The class lists in connection with the local examinations of Cambridge Uni- versity, held in December last, have just been issued, which showthat Miss C. Handley, daughter of Mr. James Hand- ley, J.P., has passed in the Junior Girls' Division with first- class honours. Miss Handley was distinguished in the following subjects :Religion, Latin, French, German, and music. Only sixteen in all England have succeeded in pass- ing this particular examination, and in the number of sub- jects Miss Handley ranks second in the list. ROBBERY FROM A PROVISION SlloP.—John Edwards, a young man of James-street, was brought before the Widnes msgistrates, on Monday, charged with having, on Tuesday, the first inst., broken into the lock-up shop of John Fitz- patrick, provision dealer, Mersey-road, and stolen 2s in money, and butter, flour, ham, eggs, pickles, &c., to the value of 138 4d. Entrance had been effected by a window at the rear of the premises, and Constable Thompson found the missing articles in various parts of the prisoner's hense.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Ses- sions for trial. HOME MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.—ID Victoria. road Chapel, on Sunday morning and evening, the Rev. W. Cuthbert, of Didsbnry, preached to goad 'congregations in aid of the Home Missionary S. cietv. On Tuesday evening the annual missionary mowing was held under the presis dency of Mr. S. Robinson, in the same place of worship. The Rev. It. Burdon mid a report, which showed that the Sum of £22 had been collected for the missions in the Widnes circuit. Addresses were deliver-fl by the Rev. J. Bryant and the Rev. J. Crozier, of Liverpool. The latter gentle- man gave an interesting account of his labours amongst the lower classes in London. The collection amounted to £3 Thud. Docs WITHOUT LICENSES AT WIDNES—At Widnes Petty Sessions on 'Thursday, before Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Wm. Thomas, of Ditton, Thoraas Duffield, James Howaid, and James Tobio were each fined Is , and costs for keeping dogs without licenses. Mr. George &pee, of Appleton, was summoned on a similar charge. He was the owner of two fox terriers, for one of which be had taken out a license, but as be had only had the other in his possession a few days he wished to try it before he took out a second license. Case dismissed. Mr. M. Bergl, of Ditton, was also charged with keeping a dog with- out license. He admitted having neglected to renew the I license at the proper time, and he called Mr. Tigbee officer of the Inland Revenue, who deposed that the defendant ' offered him the 7s 6d the day previous to the visit of the constable. He, however, dare not take the mosey. This case was also dismissed. WIDNES PETTY Sessions —At these sessions, en Thurs- day, for being drunk Walter Wilson, Patrick Mannion Mar- ,l garet Jordon, John Jones, David Dooley, James Cohester, 1 Wm. Glasheen, Elizabeth Glaeheen. were each fined.-- Michael Ryan, Ellis Worrall, and Bridget Feeley were each I convicted of committing breaches of the peace, and were bound over to be of good behaviour.-.--William Burns, a young man, Was charged with being drunk and disorderly a I with assaulting P.C. Messenger. On tbe previous even- ing the prisoner was taken into custody in Ann-street, East, on the former charge, when he struck the officer on the chest and kicked him.—lnspector Wood said the prisoner bad been before the magistrates on 22 occasions, mostly for drunkenness. For being drunk be was tined 5s and costs, and for the assault 103 and costs.--For sleeping in the chemical works of Meters. Hutchinson, Timothy Rearden. a German, and a youth named James Dwyer, were each sentenc-d to seven days' hard labour. PROLONGED STRUGGLE WITH A PRISONER AT WIDNES.— At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. John Brack and T. S. Timmie, a rough looking young fellow named George Hewitt, labourer, of Simin's Cross. was charged with having, on Saturday night, assaulted and re- sisted P.C. Luther Thompson whilst in the execution of his duty. About eleven o'clock on Saturday night the prisonee was creating a disturbance on the market ground, and the constable ordered him off. The prisoner departed in the direction of his home, and coming to a heap of stones near Dr. O'Keeffe's residence, he threw one at the constable, who was struck on the back. Thomp- son then went in pursuit of the prisoner, and capturing him behind Vine-street, a struggle which continued for 20 minutes took place. The officer was struck on the face, body, and legs, and was so exhausted with his exertions that the prisoner must have e3caped but for the fortunate arrival of Constables McDonnell and McGinis.—Mr. J. M. Knowles pleaded for the prisoner, but Mr. Brock remarked that it was an outrageous unprovoked assault, and the prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. TRANSFER DAY AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, granted the following transfers of licenses :—The Grapes 'lnn, Halton-road, from John Ormisher to William Hay- ward ; the Bins Ball, Fryer-street, from William Treverton to D tvii Snell ; the George and Dragon from John Burgess to William Jenkins; the Waterman's Arms, Weston Point, from William Hayward to William Fitton ; the Queen's Head, High-street, lately kept by Jane Baguley to John Blunt; the Royal Oak beer-house, St. John-street, from John James Newsham to Frederick George Langley; Travellers' Rest, Runcorn Hill. from William Fitton to Wm. Owen; 'the Union Vaults beer-house, Union-street, from Rickard Catton to William Santley. Joseph Thomas Blackburn, applied for permission to sell at the Albion Inn, Beel.street. Superintendent tiollingworth objected on the ground that the applicant's wife had been convicted with regard to the house two or three weeks since. The appli- cant had Since had his name placed over the door although the license was in the name of his wife. He had also failed to produce tesimonials. The Bench refused the application. Robert Goodey was granted the transfer of the license of the Bridgewater Arms. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday,lhr (i H Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children recularly to school t—William Lee, Christo- pher Evans. William Percival, Gordon McKaye Owen Rourke, Henry Anwells, John Molloy, James darrison, %oseph Davies, John Bowyer, John Coombe.% Henry Rim- mer, Thomas Mclnerney, Harriet Holland, Edward Light- foot, Jecob Ranfr, Edwin Taff, Michael Connor, Peter Ire- land, John Brannan, Charles McKenna, and Edward Price. The usual penalty of ss, including Cogs, NM imposed in each case.—Mr 'Danbv applied for Jane, the daughter of Catherine Kilalee, to be committed to an industrial School, The child had not been to school for three months, and the mother, who was a widow, had no means of main- taining the child. Her relief from the Guardians had been slopped for some reason Mr Hanby could not explain. The ^defendant said the relief was stopped because the relieving officer saw her drinking a glass of ale with-a friend of her late husband. The child was committed to the Fresbfield Industrial School.—A similar application was made in re- gard of Elizabeth, the daughter of Catherine Keenagban. In this case the girl had not a proper home, and went about the streets begging. Her parents had paid about £5 in fines for not sending her to school. An order of committal was granted, Freshfield Industrial School being selected. For all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley sad Wright's cotton Is the best.—Adet. Tint NEW R.A.—At a General Assembly of the Royal Academy held on Thursday evening, Mr. 'Luke Fildes, painter, was elected an Academician. . "SELLING BUTTRIIINE as Burritu."—Under this 1 heading we last week reported several cases in which persons were summoned for having • sold butter not of the nature and quality demanded. In the case cf Mr. A. E. A. Smith, grocer, St: Jitmes'- street, Latchford, a witness named Ashcroft was reported to have said that he was,served by Mr.s., Smith, whereas he was in reality served by the wife of the manager of the shop, who is in Mr. Smith's employ. Neithet Mr, or Mrs. Smith were at the Shop in question. ' We regret that the error should have been the means of causing Mr. Smith any. annoyanCe. FATALITY TO A NEWTON-LB-WILLOWS WOMAN.— On Tuesday a widow named Ann Pennington, 63 years of age;who lived at Newton-le-Willows, met with an accident which proved fatal. Mrs. Pen- sington went to 23, Allcard-street, off Foßy-lano, Warrington, on. Tuesday, for the purpose of attend- ing her daughter-in-law during her confinment. After having tea she went upstairs, where she re- mained until five o'clock. On coming down she slipped when near the top`of the stairs, and fell to the bottom. A. neighbour named Mary Mulvey, hearing a noise,- hastened to the place, and found deceased lying at the foot of the stairs, with her head \in the lobby an her legs on the stairs. Mul- vey lifted her up, and she poor woman, after breath- ing twice, expired. She did not speak. br. Adams wris Sent for, but his services were not re- quirec—ur. W. T. Husband, dePuty coroner, held j an inquiry into the circamstances of the death on Thursday afternoon, at the:.Rorse and Jockey Inn, Winwick-road. Evidence was given to the effect that deceased, who had lived at Mill-lane, Newton- fell downstairs and dislocated her neck. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and the Coroner remarked on the number of deaths resulting ' from falling downstairs in Warrington. Ile had held several of such inquests recently in Warrington, but none that he remembered in any other part of his district. div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODISM: WARRINGTON AND Win.. 'NES CIRCUIT.—The quarterly meeting of this cir- cuit was held in Legh-street Chapel, Warrington, on Saturday. The Rev. J. Calvert took the chair, Mr. S. Drought being appointed vice-chairman, Mr. J. Whitley secretary, and Mr. W. Crampton assistant. The circuit report for the quarter was pleasing and satisfactory. There was an increase of seven mem- bers, and after paying all demands, the steward had a balance in hand of a few pounds. The circuit's yearly report to district meeting and conference was filled up and was highly satisfactory, there be- ing an increase in every department of finance, and a total increase for the year of 27 members. The Rev. J. Calvert was appointed delegate to the dis- trict meeting, which is to be held at Preston, and Mr. Joseph Titchett vice-delegate. Mr. T. Rollason was re-elected circuit steward. Permission was given to the trustees kof Warrington chapel to pur- chase a new organ and to secure land on which to erect new chapel and schools. It was honed that the connexional year upon which they were enter- ing would be even more prosperous than the past one. WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE. The Rev. Morley Stevenson, Principal of this institution, an- nounces that the Committee of the College have decided to offer three exhibitions to students as follows :—(1) .£lO to the student who is placed highest on the list in the religious knowledge examination of candidates for admission to this college, provided she passes satisfactorily in the secular examination. (2.) £lO to the student who is placed highest in the Queen's Scholarship examination of those seeking admission to this College, provided she passes at least second class in the religious knowledge examination. (3) .C 5 to the student who passes second best in the Queen's Scholaship examination of those seek- ing admission into this College, provided she ob- tains at least a second class in the religious know- ledge examination. It is also announced that the authorities of the College are prepared to admit a limited number of students on certain conditions under article 118 n of the Education Code, which says :—" The Authorities of a College may propose to the Department for admission without examina- tion any certificated teacher who has not pirviously been trained during two years and who wishes to enter the College for a year's training in the course prescribed for students in the second year." THE MERSEY DocKs BILL.—An influential de- putation, representing municipal corporations; chambers of commerce, local boards, and other public bodies in Lancashire and Cheshire had an in- terview on Wednesday with the President of the Board of Trade in reference to the new bill of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. The object was to enlist the aid of the Government in procuring certain alterations in the constitution of that Board. It was desired that the area of residential qualifica- , tion of voters should be increased, more publicity ' given to the qualification required and the revision of the voters' lists, and the power of proxy voting restored. Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P., spoke in explanation of the objects in view, and was followed by other members of the deputation. Lord Stanley of Preston, replying said it was not the duty of his department to interfere in questions of this kind. This matter was essentially one which, in his opinion, should be fought out in Parliament. It was subsequently arranged-that Mr. Houldsworth's motion in the House of Commons with reference to the bill should stand over until Tuesday, with a view to a possible settlement. It was understood that there is every probability of a compromise be- ing arranged by which the objections of, Manches- ter to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board will be removed. LECTURE AT PENKETH.-011 Thursday evening the Rev. J. S. Balmer delivered a lecture in Penketh Chapel, to a good audience, in aid of the school ex- tension scheme, on "The characteristics of the age.' Mr. R. Garnett occupied the chair. The lecturer, who was well received, said that the people of this day were too late in the race of life to be able to develop much that is original. In almost all the regions of thought there had been men before us, and that be- ing so we could do little else but accept their man- ties. In the truest sense there was only one 'original—God, the source of all being and thought. rlf we would have that which is original we must study His work and His book. That we are too late in the race of life to develop the originality mani- fest in some of the great minds that have gone be- fore is plain enough. But, although we cannot have the originality of the great philosophers, poets, and scientists, we may have their spirit of inquiry and of effort, and may so take up what they have revealed to us as practically to make it useful. This acre is an earnest one, and he wante l it to be that the Church of Christ did not allow the world to beat it in earnestness. He would like to see the people as earnest for religion as for commerce. This ,also is an age of great wealth. It is true that money brings money, but we must not forget that it is something to spend for God, and in this wealthy age we needed to consider the uses and the responsibilities of wealth. There is a great deal of wealth of knowledge, also, in this day, but the true wealth of a nation consists in its manli- ness, its womanliness, its moral culture, •and its Christian character. Whatever our efforts to be • rich, let us try to be good. This also is an age of unrest. We are destined to advance; let our pro- gress be onward and heavenward. The restlessness he wanted to see was that which came of sympathy with lost man and zeal for Christ. The lecture was listened to with much attention.

WIDNES AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. A meeting of the " Jubilee Committee " was held at Alfon4 Chambers on Tuesday afternoon. gr. F. IL (los- sage, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were present Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. Mi wood, Conk, lityes, Handley, and Oaskell, jun., J.P.—The Chairman said he had to report and move that as there appeared to be no local interest taken in the Queen's Jubilee, the committee be adjourned sine die.—Dr. seconded the motion, and asked if it would be necessary to hold another public meeting at which to announce the decision of the committee..—The Chairman : I don't think so. Dr. O'Keeffe : I should think not.—The meeting then separated.

div.p: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.

As will be seen from the report of the business for the past year, this gigantic society continues to make extraordinary progress. The expenditure is effected with due regard for economy; in the ordi- nary branch the rate was little more than ,ten per cent on the premium income; while in the indus- trial branch there is a slight reduction in the rate of expenditure. It is exceedingly satisfactory to find on turning to the list of assets that they are of a really solid kind. The members of some societies have little more to depend on than the personal stability of the directors; but the assets of the Pru- dential include over one million sterling in 3 per cent consols, considerably over a million in free- hold ground rents, &c., and something like a million and a half on loans in municipal and other rates, be- sides Bank of Eno-land stock, railway debentures, &c. Turning to the figures we find that the assu- rance funds have been increased during the year by the sum of £1,122,054 —namely, the ordinary branch £319,496, and the industrial branch £802,558. The total assets of the company amount to £6,811,954. In the ordinary branch the number of policies issued during the year was £25,567, assur- ing the sum of £2,715,429 and producing a new annual premium income ;:if £125,604. The pre- miums of the year were £396,940, being an increase of £93,665 over the year 1885. The claims of the year amounted to £135,361. The number of deaths was 944, and 40 endowment assurances matured. The rate of expenditure of the branch was little more than 10 per cent. on the premium income. The number of policies in force was 85,089. In the industrial branch the premiums received during the year were £2,911,295, being an increase of £116,773. The claims of the year amounted to £1,123,428. The number of deaths was 133,851. The rate of expenditure of the branch shows a slight reduction. The number of policies in force, including 58,099 free policies, was 7,111,828. The quinquennial report for the period ending Decem- ber 31, 1886, shows that in the ordinary branch the annual premium income has increased from £142,732 to £407,360. The assurance fund has grown from £744,583 to £1,764,600. In the indus- trial branch the annual premium income has in- creased from £2,051,024 to £3,065,551, and the assurance fund has grown from £1,721,493 to £4,937,003, while the total assets of the company have grown from £2,580,002 to £6,811,954, being an increase of £4,231,952 in the five years under inspeetion,

The Congegational Church, Crow lane, Newton, was crowded on Tuesday forenoon, when Miss Emily Haigh Evans, youngest daughter of the late Mr. Josiah Evans, of the Reyes, Hiydock, was married to Mr. Edward Edmondsim, merchant, of Scathwaite, Blundell Sands. The interesting event was the oc- casion of unusual stir in the comparatively quiet colliery village of Haydock, and there were many 'evidences of good wishes for the happy couple. The ceremony was performed punctually at eleven o'clock, prior to which hour Mr. Alfred Caldwell, the efficient organist of the church, had rendered appropriate selections of music. The pulpit had been tastefully bedecked for the occasion with a profusion of ever- greens and spring flowers. The bride entered the sacred edifice leaning on the arm of her uncle, Mr. G. Hadfield, solicitor, of Manchester, and was accom- panied by Miss Annie Edmondson (sister of the bride- groom), Miss Roe (Manchester), Miss Cattley (Liverpool), and Miss Jessie Edmondson (sister of the bridegroom), as the bridesmaids. The c,remony was performed by the pas- tor of the church, the Rev. James Allatt, the bride being given away by her mother. As the happy couple were leaving the church, the organist played the popular'selec- tions Lohengrin's " Wedding Chorus" and Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." The bride was attired in a rich trained dress of white silk, with orange blossoms, the veil being of white tulle embroidered with Brussels lice. She wore a handsome brooch set with rubies and diamonds, and dia- monds in her hair. The bridesmaids wore dresses of pale blue satin, trimmed with bronze and lace, and white hats trimmed with blue and daffodils. The bride and each of the bridesmaids carried splendid bouquets, while each of the bridesmaids also wore a gold ring set with pearls and dia- monds, the gift of the bridegroom. As they appeared out- side the church, the newly-wedded pair were received with loud cheers On entering their carriage they drove to the Reyes, at Haydock, where a sumptuous breakfast was provided. At the entrance to the drive was a triumpnal arch bearing on one side the words " Health, happiness, and long life to the bride and bridegroom," and on the opposite side "Love, joy, and peace." Other arches were erected along the drive. The guests at the breakfast included—Colonel and Mrs McCor- qacidale, Miss A Edmondsen. Mr Massie, Mrs E Edmondson, Mr E Edmondson, jun, Mise Rim, Mr Carvt'e, Miss J Ed- mondson, Mr Comber, Miss Cattley, Mr Shelmerdine, Mr Hadfield, Mrs Edmandson, Mr Pilkington, Miss Hadfield, Mr Rimier, Miss M Edmondson, Mr Beenett, Mr E Pilking- ton, the Rev J and Mrs All att, Mrs J Edmondson, Mr Gar- diner, Mrs Deane, Mr Pollitt, Miss Edmondson, Mr and Mrs C Pilkingtoo, Miss Heyworth, Mrs Evans, Mr Edmondson, Mrs Pilkingten, Miss Browne, Mr Openshaw, Mrs Hadfield, Mrs M A Bennett, Mr A Evans, Mr Lyon, Mrs Gardiner, Mr .1 Edmondson, Mr Deane, Miss Mary Edmondson, and Mr L Pilkington. The objection is often made that the beneficial effects of proprietary medicines are only temporary, and that the disease returns as soon as the medicine is discontinued. Mr. J. It brought away about two ounces of stone; the pus has ceased to appear, the pain has vanisoed, the water is now clear, and I believe it has effected a corn. plete cure. I kave.long and fairly tried some of the ablest , medical men in South Wales., but they failed to treat the 1 case successfully, one of them remarking that medical science had failed to find a remedy for confirmed kidney disease." l Writing under date of April 27, 1896, this gentleman says : "It is now nearly four ,years since I discontinued the use of Warner's Save Cure,' and I have had no relapse of kidney trouble, have seen neither stone, gravel, nor pus during that period, no return of the bad, heavy vain in the region of the kidneys, which troubled me for years before E began the use of ' Warner's SATIR Care.' In my case the core has been thorough and permanent. and I doubt not it will be in others s;milarly afflicted if a fair trial is accorded it."

The Rev. George Waterman, Berwyn Lodge, Broadstone. About Christ- mas, 1882, I became aware of the remedy. I bad been suf- fering for two years previously from disease of the kidneys and urinary organs. During nearly the whole of that time I had been under the treatment of one of our most cele- brated London physicians, At first I derived great benefit from his skill in treatment; but at last he gave me to under- stand that he could do nothing more for me, beyond what he had already done. The statement of Dr. Hellion, of Rochester, N.Y., corning under my notice at this time, in- duced me to try IVerner's SAFE Cure." After using one or two bottles I bad a fall aealysis made of the fluid I was parsing, that I might compare it with subsequent analysis, and thus determine whether the medicine was doing me any real good or not. The first analysis showed 'albumen, by heat tests, abundant; sugar, considerable.' I continued the used of the medicine, having a fresh analysis made after each half.clizen bottles used. When I had taken 28 bottles, the last analysis showed 'no trace of either albumen or sugar by the seve et tests.' In other words, I was cured. Since then, I have recommended the medicine to several per- sons to whom I tboughtit would prove beneficial; and I have not been disappointed in a single case. The Rev. George Waterman, writing under date of April 20, 1886, is very pleased to 81,7 that it is now more than three years since he took " Warner's SAFE Cure," and he has had no return whatever of the albumen, and considers himself a perfect cure. Thousands of testimonials like the above can be shown, proving beyond the shadow of a doubt that the beneficial effects of Warner's SAFE Cure are permanent. This per- manency of Dower over disease gives it the most exalted rank, and in this particular it has no equal. THE WEST TiAWASHIRE CUP 1 COMPETITION. , 1 THE CUPHOLDER'S FIRST ROUND. ' [ET a. slum...You.] , One was inclined to think that the enthusiasm stirred up amongst the innumerable votaries of foot- ball in Warrington and the neighbouring tow is by . the competition for the West Lancashire Challenge Cup last year ;was about as intense and widespread as it well could be, but it would almost seem that it will, to use a rhetorical phrase, " sink into insignifi- cance" as compared with this ply. The attendance of spectators at St. Helens ou Saturday was some- thing to wonder at, when it is considered that it was I a first round match, and between two clubs whose 1 meeting last year was not very brimful of excitement, seeing that Warrington, metaphorically speaking, "ran away " with their opponents. But, on the . other hand, there were two or three circueistances ; which went to show that last year's result should not Ibe made too much of. In the first place, it is gener- I ally conceded that St. Helene have " played up" this year to some purpose, and are not by any means the club they were towards the close of last season. Then, again, St. Helena had the choice of ground, and vary wisely chose their own, and it is well known that footballers, like other mortals, feel all the stronger and have all the more confidence in themselves when their feet are on their native heath and the applause of their friends ringing in their ears. And last but not least, , Warrington were not in a position to put their very ; strongest team in the field, and as it turned out be- fore the game was over they were very seriously weak- ened. On the whole, indeed, it may safely be predicted I that, whether Warrington are to be the proud holders of the cup for another twelve months, or whether they have to hand it over to some successful rival, they will not have to fight a harder battle than that of Ss.tur- I day, nor is it likely that they will have to straggle under circumstances which were, taking everything into account, so dieadvantantageone. At all events the result of the encounter between the cupholders and the St. Helens aspirants to cupholding was not ' generally regarded as a foregone conclusion, and the I interest in it was On that account all the greater. Railway companies are evidently beginning to find admirers of football amongst tbeir best customers, I and on Saturday the London and North-Western offered special facilities in the shape of cheap tickets 1 , from Warrington, and these were taken advantage of by a very large number of people. On the field itself i there was a great gathering of spectators, estimated , at something like eight thousands, but as everybody knows , it is difficult to calculate very accurately the number of in- dividuals in a biz crowd, and there is always a tendency to exaggerate. But whatever might have been the exact num- ber present, there could be no mistake about the fact tbat it was a great gathering, probably the greatest that has been I recorded in the football annals of St. Helens. A glance round was sufficient to convince one that a very strong con- tingent of Warringtonians was on the ground, and this was ifurther evidenced by the hearty cheer that welcomed , Ashton and his followers Into the arena. The supporters of 1 the cupholders were glad to notice that Rigby was again to the front, apparently in the pink of condition and eager to do battle in the defence ot the t-ophy, in the winning of which he had no small share. When it was rumoured that this player was not likely to form one of the cup team this year, it was felt by everybody that the forward strength of the Warringtonians would be very considerably weakened, for Rigby is admitted on all hands to be a forward player of great strength and energy, a sure tackler, and smart at running and following up. It was, then, as might be ex- pected, no small pleasure to the well-wishers of the War.' ringtonians to see this player again in bis place, and it may here be said that his subsequent play was all that could be desired. The St. Helens captain was not many minutes behindhand in leading his men into the ring, and the en- couraging cheer that greeted them had barely died away when "business" was begun. It bad been generally re- ported that the St. Helens men were desperately in ear- nest in their resolve to haul down the colours ' of their vitors of last year, and the first few minutes plax show•d that this was the case, for never before did foot- ballers throw more energy and determination into their ex- ertions than did Borthwick's followers. This was at first especially noticeable amongst the forwards, who indeed had unusual opportunities to distinguish themselves, seeing that Warrington was weakened in this department to an alarming extent. In the first place, owing to the absence of Tolley, Fair Turner, whose powers as a forward have received county recognition, had to be placed at wing three qaarters; in the second place, Gilbert was severely injured soon after the game had begun, and his place had to be filled bf Davies, another leading and powerful forward; and, finally, later on W. Dillon, another of Warrington's picked forwards, was all but incapacitated. It will be seen, therefore, that the home team had every advantage so far as forward play was concerned, and it ,rs only fair to admit that they made the best of their chance. Several times they carried the scrimmages, but somehow or other they did not succeed so often in carrying the ball, which s ee is the cro main point. tito Itil.s related that in one of the battle lowers and King Charles' adherent, the "fiery Rupert" who led the King's cavalry broke entirely through the opposing ranks by his irresistible charges and gave chase to some fugitives, bet when he turned back again he found that the enemy had fallen upon and utterly defeated the rest of the King's army. The St. Helens forwards were "fiery Ruperts" in their way, for several times when they had broken through the scrimmages they rose only to find that their opponents had carried the ball at their toes, and were very severely pressing the home defence. On these occa- sions it was aenerally only by the smart play of the St. Helens backs that the visitors were prevented from scoring. The 4 rst part of the game was very evenly contested, and when Gilbert had to be carried off the field not a little apprehension as to the result Was felt by the admirers of the cup-holders. The lofts of a player like Gilbert, whose equal. at half-back is not often seen, was felt to be a severe I blow, especially as the play up to that time had been of so I even a character. It was soon seen, however, that the players themselves by no means felt inclined to "throw up the sponge," as they began to show increased energy and to press their opponents very severely, and when Barnes, by a most remarkable dodgy run scored the first try, there was a great display of enthusiasm. This run of Barnes, it should be stated, was really the feature of the game, as be- fore he got over the line, he had to pass nearly the whole of the opposing players. "An easy try" was the comment of

div.head: TIRDAY, MARCH l2. 1887.
div.p: TIRDAY, MARCH l2. 1887.

some df the on-lookers, bat it would have been more correct to say that it west " easy to those who knew the way," and Barnes is about the only player that football spectators in this pert of Lanceshire have the pleasure of seeing who really knows the war how to get tries of this kind. The details of the game will •no doubt be given in another column, and it is not necessary to enumerate them here, more espeeielly as no other It-tint of importance was scored. It may be enough to sty that throughout the enconuter was of the most determined character. The St. Helena men were evidently determined that it they could not score they would prevent scoring, and constantly fell on the bell when it chewed the least inclination to travel in the wrong direc• !loc. Towards the close of the game they began to find that it rats their Policy to indulge in long kicks, and by this means they pot on a couple of miners shortly before the close, but in the end the cup-holders maneged to come out with six points to three, which just secured them the victory, as a clear win by three points is needed under the rules which regulate the cup contests.

his mark, and then a series of scrimmages followed which brought about half-time, with Warrington a try and a minor to the good. Restarting, play raged in the centre, and then Speakman put in a nice pass, afterwards getting hold and kicking to touch. Ashton carried the next scrimmage, and Littlewood and Frank Turner were seen to advantage on the loose. Play now raged on the home line, but Foreman removed, Haseldon next getting in a good kick. Speakman again passed to Barnes, who scored another minor. Hasel- don next was to the fore with a nice run, being well checked by Massey. From now until the end of the game play raged in both quarters, st. Helens gaining three minors by long kick- ing. Fair. Termer collared grandly, and Massey and Speak- -man acted extremely well on the defensive. Try as they could, the Saints could not score another minor, when, ac- cording to the rules of the Union, the match would have been drawn, and after 80 minutes' play Warrington were de- clared victors by a try and two minors to three minors. It is only fair to add that Warrington got over on three other occasions, but tries were not allowed.

_ With regard to the general play it may be said to have been of the most determined character, and that it was not altogether free from roughness may be surmised from the fact that the two players above referred ta were hurt. The St. Helens team is much superior to what it was last year, and it was evidently determined to make a strong bid for the cup. Their forwards were particularly strong, and their efforts were well supplemented by the backs. Fore- man, at centre three-quarter especially played a sterling game, as aid Tickle, the full back. The Warrington team, te begin with, were somewhat crippled by the absence of Jolley, as they were thereby deprived of Fair Turner in the forward department, and after Gilbert's retirement they were still worse off. It was only by splendid all- round play that they managed to come off victors. Barnes played a splendid game, and the manner in which be ob- tained the try was something to witness. At the wings' Fair Turner NIS useful in tackling, and Massey, by his quickness stopped some dangerous rushes. Appleton also showed up well, but coneidering the strenuous nature of the game, the wing three-quarters and full back had compare.- tively little to do. At half-back Gilbert did some good ser- vice during the short time he was on the field, and through- out Speakman was indefatigable, and thwarted many a dangerous onset. Davies also played a determined game as Gilbert's substitute. It would be almost unfair to single out any of the forwards when all did so well, but it may be said that Rigby, Aehton, and Frank Turner were particu- larly prominent. Teams :—St. Helens :—Full back, A Tickle; three-quarter backs, W Hasledon, E Foreman, and J Halton ' • halt-back, T Finney and C Anders; forwards, A Borthwick (captain), H Varier, R Leatherbarrow, J Basdett, T Pennington, R Ellison, D McLonghlan, J Harwood, and J Dearden. War- rington : Full back, Appleton; three-quarter backs, Fair. Turner, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Gilbert and Speak- man ; forwards, Ashton (captain). Frank Thrner, rovey, Littlewood, Davies, Hough, E Dillon, W Dillon, and Rigby. ST. HELENS RECREATION V. BOOTLE. _ _ .

The St. Helens Recreation football team Journeyed to Bootle, on Saturday, for the purpose of trying conclusions with the Bootle team in the first round of the West Lan- cashire Cup, stud the result showed that they were emi- nently more fortunate than their townsmen with the War- ringtonians, decisively beating their opponents on all points of the game. The home team having won the toss, opened play by a good kick, and following up the ball at once, forced the visitors to tonah down. This point was the first and last for Bootle. The " Recs." against a slight breeze played in excellent form. Pilkington, Langley, and J Gregeon were the first to distinguish themselves. The latter, in attempting to drop at goal, kicked dead. From the drop out, the "Recs." again penned their opponents, Bootle having to save. Shortly afterwards J. Rankin placed the oall under the goal posts in fine style. From the place, Gaskell kicked a goal. Re-start- ing, a free kick fell to Pilkington, bringing the ball into touch near the home team goal line. From the line-out Pdkington got a try, and Gaskell kicked the second goal. Turning round, the visitors played a sterling game, and ir- resistably penned their opponents in their own twenty-five nearly the whole of the second half. Bottle endeavoured to play a saving game, and touched down no less than seven times. The " Recs." played a desperate game, and in quick succession Cook, Hankinson, Langley, Gaskell, Ashton, and Smith, each gained a try. J. Pilkington landed a goal • from flankinson's try. Final score : Recreation, three goals, five tries, nine minors, or fifty-three points; to Bootle, one miner, or one point. The tame were as follows: Si, Helens Recrea- tion: W E Taylor, back; J Pilkington, R Langley and J Gregson, three-qu.rter backs; A Smith and W Parr (cap- tain), halt-backs; T Green, W Cook, R Twist, W Dean, J Pyke, H Gregson, J Gaskell, H Ashton, and James Hankin- son, forwards. Bootle: Stanley Riddock, back; James Rirldock, H Johnson, and J Enema, three-quarter backs; William Shaw and C Fox. half-backs; H Barker, A Pad- dock, B Spedding, A Brown, A Foster W Pendleton, S Fowler, W Hicks, and F Jackson, forwards. WIDNES v. BLACKROD.

These teams met at Widnes on Saturday,' when the home team were declared winners by 25 points to two (one goal, two tries, and nine minors, to two minors.) During the first half, play was very tame, Widnes only scoring three minors to their opponents one; but with the ckange of ends a change took place in the character of the game. No sooner had Kiddie kicked off than the ball was rushed to the home line and kicked dead. After the return, Plumpton ran splendidly and grounded the ball over the Blackrod line, but the place kick was difficult, and Kiddie failed to improve matters. Widnes having added two minors, Ridyard secured another try, after fine runs by Plumpton and Howard. Kiddie again failed at the place. Plimpton maUe a brilliant shot at goal soon after, the ball missing by a foot; and then Wmpils obtained the thirn try, as the result of a fine dribble by Ridyard and Pervin. This was an easy place, and Farrel landed a fine goal. Wid- nes continued to pile on minors and the game ended as above stated. Harding was injured at the commencement, and in consequence was of no use.

Teams '—Widnes: S Bingham, back; Harding, Plump. ton, and Pennington, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Howard, half-backs; Kiddie (captain), Smi,h, Woods, Rid. yard, J Bingham, Hughes, Pervin, Fogg, and Corns, for- wards.
