RoNC,MS V. SaLFOßD.—Notwithstanding the great in- terest created by the West Lancashire Cup ties and other attractions, upwards of 4,000 spectators put in an appear. ance at the Runcorn ground taewitnese the play between the Cheshire champions and the victors in the recent match with the Swinton fifteen. W. Hughes eterted what proved a magnificent game, with the sun in his eyes. Btarterworth ran the ball beck to centre, and Roberts was celled upon to check Speakman. Some hot scrimmages were waged about the centre, when during a geveral scramble over the home line Jackson fell on the ball, scoring firat for Salford. The kick at goal, however, failed. From a line-out Roberts tried to get away, bet Lewis and Faulkner tackled well, and Salford touched down. Speakman returned Varley's drop out, and kicked hack to the Salford quarters. Bit by bit the ball was carried near the Salford line, until Hughes threw tO Davies. Butterworth having intercepted, the visi- tors' forwards broke away. when Broady and W. Hughes retaliated, Cowley making further progress. The play con- tinued in the Salford half, and hereabouts H. Hughes got away, and by a spirited 'run reached the line safely, grounding the bell, and Broady kicked a grand goal. Oa Ottiwell kicking off, Faulkner returned lute touch. From the line-out Runcorn fought their way to- wards tbe Salford goal. Varley kicked back, to which Davies replied and ran strongly, kicking in touch. Speakman dropped at goal shortly afterwards, bat only a minor point was gained. Play was continued with great vigour, and Sp,ikman, passing to perfection, threw out to Cawley, who deshed over the line close to the corner flag. Broady took the place, and kicked a splendid goal from the touch line. Halftime was called directly after, the score being Runcorn two goals to Salford one try. Ottivrell restarted the ball, Cowley returning, the game still being =tested with great spirit. Varley made an attempt at goal, which wee smartly charged down, although Speak• man was forced to save a little later on. Still the pace of the game was maintained, the following up and maenificent pwsing of the Runcorn torwards—Lewis, Hughes, Faulkner, and Wright—cot tributing in a great measure to the victory. gothiog further of value was scodre, and one of the grandest and most pleasantly-contested games seen at Runcorn ended in a victory for the home team by two goals and four minor points to Salford one try and three minor paints. For !tele- com every men seemed to be in his best form. Speakman played a truly magnificent game, El Hughes being in excel. lent form at half beck. The forwards worked like Trojans, their passing and following up being a treat. The Salford men played bard, but the pace was a bit too fast for them. Varley did a lot of work at centre three-quarters, and Roberts, Williams, and Jackson worked herd in the mauls. The teams were as follows :—Runcorn : T Woods, back; H Cawley, H C Speakman, and T Davies, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and HG Andrews, half backs ; IV Wright. W H Broady, W Hughes, W Faulkner, J Lewis, J Barns, J Gat- ley, George Wainwright, and J Clarke, forwards. Salford : Mainwaring, back ;. Walmeley, Varley, and Butterworth. three-quarter backs; Clegg and Newton half backs; Barlow, Ottiwell, Hughes, Shaw, Roberts, Stott, Vickers, and Smith, forwards. WARRINOTON "A " TEAM V. BLUNDELLSaNDS, IST. Owing to Blerndellsande not arriving until four o'clock a game was arranged between 20 of St. Paul's and the War. rington "A " team, and after half-an-hour's play Warring- led by one try (Antrobne) and two minors to one minor. At 4.15 Green kicked oft for Blundellsands, Whittle re- turning into breach. Immediately after the line out Uns- worth got hold and put in a good kick, and, following up, collared Dalton before he could return. Eves, Cragh an, and Bandies broke away with a dribble, and Nevins obtained a free kick, the ball going into touch. Whittle got posses. sion from the line out, and passed to Beishaw, who gave the ball to Boardman. The latter player, after making a short run, kicked into touch. The ball was next passed to Nev- ins, who dribbled close to the line, but kicked too herd, and the ball went dead. Hackett was afterwards conspicuous with a good dribble, and Whittle made a good run and passed to Belshaw, who eras stopped by Freeman. Shortly afterwards Nevins was allowed a free kick for offside tack- ling, the ball going into touch in the visitors' 25. The borne forwards, headed by Jones, Craghau and Randlee, dribbled to the line. Clark being compelled to touch down. From the drop out the visitors worked the ball to centre, where Belshaw gave‘the oval to Nevins, who punted it to touch. Antrobue next got possession from a scrimmage, and made a good run, finishing up by punting to Clark, who made a poor return. Tbornley kicked the ball over the line, and Handles, following up, gained a well- mer:ted try. Boardman made a good attempt at goal. Green re-started, Jones returning into touch. Whittle passed to Belshaw, who, on being tackled, threw the ball to Boardman, but Altv intercepted the pass and took play down the field, Jolley saving well. The visiting forwarde now broke a way, and dribbled to the home 25, Whittle sav- ing. From the scrimmage which ensued, J. Roughley got hold and dropped a goal, this performance being applauded by the spectators. Whittle kicked off, and Eyes, Lloyd, and Howarth took play to the visitors' 25, Freeman reply- ing with a long punt and Jolley returning well. Tbornley Jones, and Hackett dribbled the ball to the line, and Nevins had a good chance of scoring, but he kicked rather too hard, the ball going dead. Shortly after the drop out Bel. shaw, Unsworth, and Thornlev worked the bell to the visi- tors' lines. forcing Blundellsends to again save by touching down. Half-time was called, the score standing Blundell. sands, 1 goal, Warrington I try and 3 minors. On resum- ing, play for some time was of a very even character. Eventually Lloyd, Unsworth, and Whittle broke away with a grand dribble, and the last-named player succeeded in grounding the ball over the line, Boardman kicking a goal. Green kicked off, Play resting in centre. Whittle, Craghan' and Unsworth again broke away, but Roughley neutralised their efforts by kicking into touch. Freeman next got hold from a pass by Ronghlev, and made a good ran, being brought down by Boardman. Lloyd now made a splendid dribble, taking the ball over the line, and Unsworth rush- ing up, gained a try between the posts. Boardman failed at the place. From a scrimmage on the line the visitors. were forced to concede another minor. Time was called shortly afterwards, leaving Warrington winners by one goal, two triem, and four minor points, to Blundellsands one dropped goal. Teams :Warrington: Full back. Jolley ; three-quarter backs, Nevins, Bele:law, and Boardman; half-backs, Antrobus and Whittle (captain) ; forwards, Cra- ghan, Jones, Hackett, Eyes, Thornlev, Lloyd, Unsworth, Howarth, and Handles. Blandellsands : Full back, Clark; three-quarter hacks, Freeman, Alt, and Dalton ; half-backs Leonard and J. Raughle9 forward,, T. Green, J. Leonard, Hidlinson, Mawdsley, Bothwell, T. and E. Deolin, Brew, and H Wright. Referee. Mr. T. Pemberton. WEST LANCATSIHOE—FCIREALTLREONITGNEDCUP COMPETI- WARRINGTON V. ST. HELENS. On Saturday the first rounds in the competition for the West Lancashire and Border Towns Union Challenge Cup were played eff. Last year the cup was won by the Warrington Football Club. in whosa keeping, of coarse, it still is. With regard to none of the matches in this round was there more interest shown than in that between the cupholders and St. Helens, on the ground of the latter. It is estimated that between two and three thousand persons went from War- rington to witness the contest, and in the field itself there were probably about 6,000 spectators. The Warrington team was hort of Jolley, whose place at three-quarter was s taken by Fair Turner, and in the course of the match two of the team were hurt, namely, Gilbert, a sinew of whose leg, it is understood, has been broken, and W. Dillon sustained severe injuries to his ribs. Gilbert's injuries were con- sidered to be of so serious a nature that he was sent to the Infirmary at Liverpool. A start was made ahont twenty minates to font o'clock by Frank Tamer kicking off, the ball going into touch. A scrimmage was next formed in the St. Helens 25, their for- wards removing to centre. The Warringtonians worked the ball down the field and compelled Halton to touch down. Fair Turner next collared Haseldon, and then Leatherbarrow and Pennington broke away to Warrington quarters. Rigby, how- ever, came through with a good dribble, Tickle kicking to touch. Some good play on the parts of Halton and Foreman took play to Warringten quarters. Gilbert was hurt at this juncture of the game, and had to retire, Davies taking his place at half. W. Dillon now got in a tidy run, and a free kick was acceded to Warrington. Fair. Turner then led off with a good kick, being followed by good forward play on , the parts of the forwards. Davies pot In a goed pass to Barnes, who kicked to Haseldon, who was collared. Massey then kicked to touch. Speakman now passed nicely Co Barnes, who made a splendid dodgy run, and g .ined the only try of the match. amidst the wildest excitement. Frank Turner failed to kick a goal. From the kick out Riehy showed up prominently with a dribble, Foreman re- plying with a good run and kick, Barnes kicking to touch. Anders next put in a neat pass to Foreman, but Barnes spoiled his chances of making headway. Tickle next made

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

As was expected, Warrington —woji-n" their encounter with St. Helens, but it was scarcely expected that they would win only by the bare majority of points. Though beaten, St. Helens were by no means disgraced, and the match has rather added to their renown than taken from it. It must be said, however, that if ever they had a chance of beating Warrington it WAS last Saturday, as fate seemed to fight against the cupbolders. It was only by sterling play on their part that the disadvantages they had to suffer under Were overcome.

Gilbert and Dillon, the two of the Warrington team who were injured, are we are pleased to hear, progressing favourably. Gilbert has been vcry unfortunate lately in the matter of injuries, and it is a pity that it should be so, for a fairer and more unselfish player, and one who acquits himself in a more gentlemanly fashion, never entered the football field.

The excitement that seems to pervade tbe local football world with regard to the meeting to-day of Warriagton and Widnes has probably never been paralleled. That the game will be keenly fought goes without saying. Widnes are playing the same team which beat the cupholders a short time ago, while Warrington will be short of Gilbert and Dillon. Looking at it in this way, it might seem that the odds were on Widnes, but, taking everything into account, we should be inclined to predict that Warrington will come out of a very close and exciting contest with a few points to the good. It should be noted that a very good likeness of Harry Ashton. the Warrington captain, adorns the front page of the" Football Times" this week, and there is also a short biography of his career as a footballer. Ashton well de- serves this distinction, for the period of his leadership has been a very sarcessf uI one.

As was anticipated, Widnes had an easy task in vanquish- ‘ing Blackrod in the first round of the West Lancashire Cup competition. The form displayed in the first half was cer- tainly not up to the standard of cup winners, but no doubt the accident to flarding a few minutes after the commence- ment of the gams, which rendered him practically utiles% disorganised the team to some extent. In the second half mere combination and dash was shown, and a rather heavy score was piled up. At ne part of the game, however, did the team show anything like the form which enabled them to defeat Warrington and Mpull. A less desire to achieve individual distinction, and more unselfish passing amongst both for wards and backs, would place Widnes in the front rank of clubs, as for speed and stamina they are now bad to beat.

Runcorn put the crowning point upon their victorious career on Saturday, when they rnade the crack Salford team taste the bitters of defeat. Having defeated Swinton a couple of weeks ago, Salford were setting up a claim to be the champions of the county palatine, and the jubilant Runcorn folks are new inquiring what position the wearers of the green must be assigned in the football world. They have npw beaten every club they have met during this sea- son, in fact have only lost one match, and that at Salford at an early period, and before they had settled into their form. Snch a record is one to be proud of, and it is to be hoped that conscious of their strength they will not on some occasion be caught napping, and thus have their colours lowered.

Combination and unselfish passing was the cause of Runcorn's success, and had not the Salford captain adopted the defensive tactic of placing four three-quarter backs to intercept the passes during the second half of the match, the scare against his team would have been much heavier than it was. A feature of the match was the line goal kick- ing of Broady, who landed the Sphere over the bar twice, once from one of the most difficult places imaginable. The want of a goal kicker was Runcorn's one weak spot; per- haps now they have found him. The sixteenth annual international game between Eng- land and Scotland was played on Saturday at Whalley Range, Manchester, in the presence of an immense num- ber of spectators. Of the previous matches six have been won by England, three by Scotland, and six have been drawn. In four of the drawn games neither side scored. This year the Indications all pointed to a victory for Scot- land, whose team has just recently beaten Ireland very de- cisiyely,whilst the English representatives had been worsted by the .13hoys." la the result, however, another contest was added to the list of draws, tuough the game ended slightly in favour of Scotland by one tr y,and three minors

to one try and one minor. Tha play was to a great extent spoiled by the dense fog which overhung the ground, and enveloped the players in invisibility to a large number of the spectators. The English learn was composed as fol- lows:—H 13 Tristram (Durham), back; W N 13,1t0n (Black- heath), R Robertstiaw (Bradford), and R Lockwood (Dews- bury), three-quarters; A Rotherham (Richmond) and F Bonsor (Bradford) half backs; J H Dewhurst (Cambridge University). W G Clibborn (Richmond). G L Jeffrey (Blackheath), C R Cleveland (Oxford University), J L Hickson. E Wilkinson (Bradford), R L Seddon, A Teggin (Broughton Rangers), and H Sprigmann (Liverpool) forwards.

In Association circles tbe defeat on Saturday of the Preston North Endue bY West Bromwich Albion in the semi-finals for the English cup was a rather unexpected event. The game took place at Trent Bridge ground, Not- tingham, and the widespread interest that was centred in it was evidenced by the presence of something like sixteen , thousand spectator.. The Prestonians, as might to expect- ed, did not succumb easily, and the Albion owe their vic- tory of three goals to one as a large degree to their splendid defer's' ye powers. To some of the matches in the first round of the West Lancashire Challenge Cup competition we refer at length in our report columns, but the following is a complete sum- mary of the results :—Warrington beat St. Helens by a try and two minors to three minors, at St. Helene; Widnes beat Blackrod by one goal, two tries, end nine minor, to two minors, at Widnes; St. Helens Recreation beat Bootle by three goals, five tries, and nine minors to one minor, at Bootle; Aspult beat Southport Olympic by two goals, two tries, and six minors to a goal and two minors, at Aspull ; Wigan beat Litherland by two goals, two tries, and two , minors to a try and four minors, at Litherland ; Walkden beat Leigh by five points to two, at Walkden; TyldesleY beat Tuebrook by eleven minors to two minors, at Tue. br•ok ; and Walton beat Liverpool Wanderers by two tries and four minors to two minors. At 3 meeting of the West Lancashire Committee, at Liverpool, on Saturday last, the following draws were made for the second round of the com- petition, viz. :—Aspull v. St. Helens Recreation. Referee, Mr. Lord, Broughton. Warrington v. Widnes. Referee, Mr. A. Durandu, Liverpool. Walkden v. Wigan. Referee, Mr. Kneen, Broughton. Walton v. Tyldesley. Referee, Mr. Crenshaw, Wigan. Thee ties will be played off to-day (Saturday).

MUSEUM FREE LECTURES.

On Monday evening, the last of the series of free lectures in connection with the Warrington Museum was delivered in the Lecture-room, Museum-street, by the Rev. J. Yonge ; subject, "Working-class England: fifty years ago and now." Alderman Webster presided, and there was again a full atten- dance. At the outset of his lecture' Mr. YONGH mentioned that the reference In the title of his lec- ture to "fifty years ago" had been 'suggested by the queen's jubilee. That was a period in our national history to which the /public mind'is now largely directed. Everyone is talking, from some ' motive or other, of .the jubilee of the queen's reign. • The celebration of that jubilee is agitating all places in all parts of the empire, and all sorts of schemes are being projected to effect the pur- pose. An imperial institute which hangs fire; and a Church house; which is likely to be as unsubstan- tial and unrealised as a castle in the air; a women's I offering to the queen, which will probably find some shape, equestrian or otherwise—these appeared so far the principal national tributes which have been devised. Each separate locality of course; is busy considering' what most it can do to benefit itself by making capital out of the royal jubilee. One village has de- termined upon a public pump (laughter) -- another town, a very Welsh one, . has resolved upon the pleasant acquisition of a cemetery. (Laugh- td.) Our own loyal borough is distracted by ear- nest advocacy of rival schemes which are still under discussion. Beyond a general understanding that the jubilee involves a public holiday and a demon- stration, a feed for old folk, and fireworks for the young, no more permanent plan has yet been agreed upon. Whether a bath, 'a ragged school, a statue, or a new park railing, a larger chamber for the local parliament $ or a library free to all ratepayers—(ap- plause)—still' awaits decision. Speaking on those premises he 'nigh t perhaps, in passing, be permitted to avow his personal preference for the scheme last named, as being at once more' widely popular and more generally useful than'. the rest. (Applause.) it was remarkable, however, that the whole of the proposedschemes for the celebration of the jubilee throughoutthe country are much of the nature of the Englishman's toast, which' once occasioned great amazement to a foreigner. "I observe" he "that John Bull has a curious way of making and drinking a toast. First, he puts in whisky to make it strong; then water to make 'weak. Next he puts in sugar to make it swee,t, then lemon to make it sour. And then he says 'Here's to you,' and drinks it himself." (Laughter.) So we were all complimenting the queen, and benefitting our- selves.. (Hear, hear.) The great occasion of the jubilee would serve a good purpose if popular at- tention became directecl to the progress and d 3 velopment which the nation had achieved in the half 'century now drawing td a close. That progress viewed as a whole, throughout all departments and realms of the national and Imperial life is probably without parallel in the history of the world. And perhaps in no one of the many sections of the com 4 munity is that progress more marked and 'marvel- lous than among the working classes. That institu- tion in which they were itself was an illustration of the enlarged privileges and opportunities for men- tal and social improvement which exist now as compared with 50 years ago. (Hear, hear.) It might almost be said to be still in its infancy, and good as it was, it mi. 414 hare been better if it had received more generous diet. But when a larger public spirit began to .prevail among the richer classes of the locality, we might expect that Museum and Library to underip rapid develop- ment. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He ventured to submit that ono great need of their good town was more enterprise and public spirit among its leading men. (Hear, heas,) Coming to the aim of the leture, Mr. Yonge Aid that probably the story of fifty years ago, which he should try in part in tell, would be almost new to many in that room. If so, it would probably be surprising. It might almost seem impossible that things could ever have been so bad as`they 'were then. We had come now to the time when power and privilege were no longer the exclusile possession of any class, but of all classes. (Hear, hear.) If there be a _preponderance of power now, it is in the hands of that class whieh fifty years ago had none. This is unquestionably the day of the working class. At least it is the dawning of the day, and working men are eagerly longing for the full glories of the 'noontide. Some of them might have read how Macauley, in his history, described the condition of Ithe working class of this country 200 years ago. Then, 6d a day was all that could be earned by hard labour and lon hours at the loom; and 'a "work- man employedmi the great- staple manufacture of England thought himself fairly,pairlif he gained -68 amteek.' At •that t time it was estimated that the working people og ,England numbered "800,000 families. Of these families 440,000 ate a'aimal food twice a week. The temainder ate it not at all, or, s,t mast, not oftener than once a week." It would not be far wrong to say that description, in the main, was as true of 50, as of 200 years ago, although no doubt there had, in the interval, beeh some improvement and advance. Referring to the early years of this century, the lecturer said that want of work was by no means the only evil that characterised the condition of the industrial classes at the period under. review. The 'conditions of work were as bad as could possibly be, and the life of a working man was little if any better than the life of a bond slave. Up to very nearly the commencement of the Queen's reign it was illegal for working-men to combine in defence of their own interests. An Act had been passed nearly 500 years before, namely 1350, which made it criminal for working people to enter into any combination, the object of which was either to raise wages or reduce the hours of labour. Not un- til 1824 was this Act of the old days of bondage, and , the power of the few to grind down the many re- pealed and excised from the statute book. But from the days of its repeal hope began to rise up in the workman's heart, and he has since gone on at first in slow, but now in quickening progress to- wards the rights and liberties of his manhood. (Applause.) The lecture throughout was evidently of great interest to the audience and was frequently ap- plauded.—After the lecture, Alderman WEBSTER said that the attendance at that series of lectures had been eminently satisfactory, having exceeded the , expectations of the committee. He was in hopes , that next season they would be able to make ar- rangements for # longer series. (Hear \ hear.) There was another experiment which the committee wished to try to popularise that institution. It was proposed to have a series of what they might call museum talks or conversations and not formal lec- tures. The contents of the museum would form a very interesting basis of these' conversations which would, of course, be held in the museum. (Hear, hear)" The first of these gatherings, he mentioned, would be held at the Museum to-night (Saturday) at seven o'clock in the antiquities department,—The proceedings then crcludet

-------- , A woman is keeping in a book a list of things she ought to purchase but cannot afford to wear. She calls the book her ought-to-buy-ography. Socrotoorcm..—The man who lives on little is wor- shipped as an economist, while he who lives on nothing is despised as a tramp. " FIXING " AN EDITOR.—A female contributor who was called to account by an editor for writing on both sides of her paper retorted, "Well, and don't you print on both sides of yours?" A good story is told of a rough specimen of a colonist who was over here for the Colinderies." On being pointed out Waterloo Station, he remarked, "Really ! Was that where the battle was fought?" • I THE REAL DIFFICULTY.—A witty woman of Palm says that it is more difficult for a woman to make excuses for her beauty among other women when she is really beautiful, than for a plain woman to And favour among the men. Nov A DELIGHTFUL SENSA.TION.—A criminal was bailed out in New York, the other day, who vows he wouldn't have the process repeated for 1,000 dollars. It was done with a stomach pump. A WOMAN'S REASON.—" It's bitterly cold," said a hus- band, with a shiver; "why don't you button up your fur-lined circular?" " Bec,ause I want it to fly open," replied the lady, placidly. The female high hat at the theatre is an exhibition of bad taste that we could easily overlook—if the management would kindly provide, us with a step- ladder. The Queen of Roumania, it is said, frequently de- livers private lectures to her maids. Other women are very like the Queen, only they do riot confine their lec- tures to their maids. , „ Lr„ TOBOGGANING HAS A 14'm:rm.—First Sweet - e you like tobogganing ?" Second Sweet Girl: "Not so much as dancing." •' Neither do I." "No, it's too long between hugs." An old lady said that she could not tell her mince-pies from her apple-pies without cutting them, ri,nd was ad- vised to mark them. She did so, and remarked com- placently, "This I've marked 'T. M.'77''Tis mince '— and that T. M.'—' 'Taint mince.' A NOTABLE REMNANT.—Another member of the im- mortal "Six Hundred" has just died. There must have been about 1,300 of them when they went into the fight, I and some 3,000 must have come out alive to account for the numerous mortality since. A Boston woman who has kept a boarding-house for thirty-eight years figured up the profits the other day, and found that they wouldn't buy her a sun-bonnet. She says she must have furnished too good beefsteak, though she always asked for neck pieces. Of five people who, on their dying beds last year, con- fessed to their crimes, only one told the truth, in the other cases it was shown that the "confessors" could not possibly have had anything to do with the crimes. There- are death-bed cranks as well as cranks in good health' A tourist who had left a waterproof coat in a train at Inverness Station went back to look for it. He asked the occupants of a third-class compartment if they had seen a black macintosh there. a," one of the occupants responded;. "we're a' "Na,;IA Macphersons

here." Tins LABoon MAnzier.—Broom : "Well, Bill, 'ow are you gettilf on ?" Shovel: "Oh, I dunno ; I ain't doin' nothm' pertikler! I wus a-gettin' on fust-rate as one of the unemployed, when the frost broke up, an' I was obliged to take on a job." WHEN GIRLS OUGHT TO MARRY.—" No," said a fond mother, snaking proudly of her twenty-five-year-oli daughter— no, Mary isn't old enough to marry yet. She cries whenever any one scolds her; and until she becomes hardened enough to reply vigorously she isn't fit for a wile." "John B. Alley, of Massachusetts, lunches on bread and milk, price sixteen cents. That is why he is able to draw his check for twenty millions," says an ex- change. That's nothing. As anybody can tell spirits from the vasty deep, so anybody can draw his check for i twenty millions. The rub is the same in both cases— will they come? A EASIER TRIM—An/Hungarian conjurer spreads a newspaper upon the floor and places a young woman upon it, whom he covers with &piece of silk and then causes to disappear. We have never seen this trick here, but we have known a man to put 50,000 dollars on a newspaper and itc has disappeared before he could Cover it with anything. This was Charles Lamb's rebuke to a man who by self- assertion pronunced himself devoid of any peculiarity; " Wh-which hand do you b-b-blow your n-n-ose with?" inquired Lamb. "With my right hand, to be sure." "Ali," said Lamb pensively, that's your pe-pe-eullarity ! I b-b-blot mine with my latandkerchief." HOPED IT WAS PERMANENT.—"I am struck dumb at your conduct 1" exclaimed Mrs. Dempsey as her hus- band tottered into the house at 2 a.m. the other night after playing a tatoo with the latchkey all over the door. "W—well, my dear," was the cheerful response, "I'm. sure I h—hope it's a permanent strike." COMMON SENSE IN LITER.ATIIRE.—Ppening sentence Ella Wheeler Wilcox's story of Perdita, now published in book form: "Leaning over the broken stile, just at the edge of a wood, a girl stood straining her eyes through the gathering gloom." On the whole this was better than if the dear girl had strained her eyes through a sieve. • A BAD PRACTICE.—Dr. X. is called to see a patient. "Things are not all right with me, doctor." "What is the matter?" "Why, all night long I seemed to be flying around through space; couldn't sleep—bad dreams." "What did you eat for dinner?" "A pigeon." " Ah, that accounts for it! One of those carrrier-pigeons too, no doubt, Bad practice, my dear sir. Don't do it again." As NEAR AS HE COULD GET TO IT.—Actors on Union

Square. "Can you give me that ten dollars, Jaggers ?" "What ten dollars ? " "The ten dollars you borrowed on the road." "All right, my boy. I'll pay it to you in fe nor other." "Well, make it as like ten dollars

-- THE JUBILEE CELEBRATION IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—A. question that is being rather anxiously asked by people who take any interest at all en the Jubilee, is whether the town as a whole is to have any voice in the affair, or whether it is to be entirely managed by the limited number of persons who were invited by the Mayor to dis- cuss the matter. These persons have been "called up" by the civil chief of the town after the manner in which despotic potentates used to call up a few of their subjects when they wished to have a kind of popular assent to the carrying out of schemes already fixed upon. They cannot in any way be looked upon as having sty representative authority, as they are where they are merely by "the grace of the Mayor." It their function is merely to consider and discuss various projects, and finally to decide upon recom- mending one or more to a meeting open to all—rich and poor alike—who can lay claim to a voice in what is really a matter affecting the whole town, then they will serve a use- ful purpose. If, on the other hand, it is not intended to call a Town's Meeting, bat to carry the matter through on the sole authority of this officially-selected committee, it is to be feared that it will he looked upon as a kind of hole- and-corner business. I presume the people of the town le a whole will be invited to contribute towards the expenses of the celebration, but if they have had no voice either directly or through those whom they look upon as their representa- tives, they cannot be expected to "stump up" very liberally. M.

TIIE MARKET AGITATION. Sir,—As one that has watched with interest the doings of our Market Committee since the opeoiag of our new market, lam at a loes to understand the next move. It will cer- tainly not be for the interest and comfort of our stall holders who are called upon to pay high rents, besides rates, in the borough, and, then have to compete with so- called fruiterers, or a penny an article, to retail out against a 6a or 7s per week gall-bolder. In fact, our Market Commit- tee's aim almost appears to be anything and everything , mixed tip together so long as money is rolling in. As a ratepayer, I really thought from the various debates in the Council we were going to have the markets perfectly ar- ranged, only it would take a few months to do it, we were told. But years are now gone by, and the arrangements are worse to-day than then. At the opening of the new market, a certain allotment was made to our fruiterers; IS stalls were then sold. 65 per week,l believe, being the committee's reserve bid. The prices have run as high as 9s per week, the result being that only about four still retain their stalls, for reasons best known to them- selves, since their separation from the butchers. I trust they will learn a lesson from the fruiterers' removal. The in- tention of the committee of having a wholesale market to close at a certain gives time pas proved a failure so far, and serious loss financially to them. Again, who could walk through our new market in the summer months without feeling for the farmer's wife—to see her butter melting with the oppressive heat of so lew a shed? It was not so before in the hall, which is cool and
lofty, besides serving as an introduction to the butchers and ether business people. Wishing every success in the forma- tion of a Ratepayers' Association, I remain. your,. &c., A RATEPAYER.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. HOWES. Sir,—When I received Mr. Chamberlain's letter on the 22nd ult., I wrote to Mr. Howes the same day, and sent him a copy of it. I asked him to send me the exact words of that part of Lord Salisbury's speech which be quoted at Warrington, and if he still adhered to his statement that Mr Chamberlain bad not condemned the principle of that speech, before I published Mr. Chamberlain's letter. But I did not receive a reply from Mr, Howes till the 28th tilt. He then informed me that he bad sent his reply to the 'Daily News" in order to lave time. I received another letter from him last Friday night, asking me if! had come across any of Mr, Chamberlain's speeches where he had re- pudiated Lord Salisbury's views. I have not been able to come across Mr. Chamberlain's speech on the quettion, hav- ing unfortunately lot it; but I still adhere to my state• ment that Mr. Chamberlain had in speech, since August 190, 1888, said that he could not support Lord Salisbury if he attempted to carry out a plan of that kind, viz, that if the tenant farmers of Ireland were unable to comply with the conditions laid down by the Land Act of 1881, that the State should bear the loss, and not the landlords. I have asked others who strongly support Mr. Gladstone's Irish measures if they could remember it, and they expressed themselves in the affirmative. I am surprised that Mr. Howes still persists in trying to lead the public to believe that Mr. Chamberlain is inconsistent with his well-known and oft expressed opinions against buying out the land at the risk of the British taxpayer. Trusting that Mr. Howes will cease to misrepresent further Mr. Chamberlain, I re- main, yours respectfully, March 9th, 1887. L. SUTCLIFFE. [Mr. Sutcliffe expresses his willingness to di.cuss with Mr. Taylor the subject of Mr. Gladatone's Irish Land Bill, but we cannot at present make room for such a debate.--• ED. E 2.1

Mv dear Sir,—l notice in the "Live-ruff-A Echo "of this evening a letter purporting to emanate from von to a "War- rington correspondent" respecting a reference of mine to Tour recent vote regarding the Procedure Rules and Welsh bisestablishment. Ido not know what the terms of your correspondent's letter may have been, to have led you to the use of such strong language, but I certainly do not plead guilty of Injustice whatever may be the Case as to my " ig- norance." I did not say that you voted against the prtn- crple of religions equality. Your name was casually men- tioned as an illustratise of the fact .that even great and good men may change their opinions in course of time. I. took care to assert that the reference had no political signi- ficance,and that I expressed no opinion upon the vote itself Perhaps your correspondent did not state this. But, sir, since the question has been raised, you will permit me is say that not only I. but a vast number besides of those who have loved and revered you, as I have done, perceive with the deepest sorrow that your dissension from the majority of the Liberal party on the Irish question is so extreme as to lead you to give such a vote as you did the other night. Impugn your motives we cannot ; regretting your action, we cannot help.—Youse very truly, EDWARD MOORE. , RT. How. JOHN BRIGHT, EEQ M.P.,
Rochdale.

ENGLAND AND EGYPT. Sir,—The custom at the present time seems to be *ir- "nal inI4ITY• The Tory working-man bears something that he cannot comprehend, and forthwith writes off to a .‘ disinterested " Duke, Lord, or Rt. Hon. Gentleman. I am sorry to eee we find the Radical working-man apeing the manners of the Tory, and writing to the Rt. Hon. Gen- tleman to tind ant if a certain statement is or is not true. This seem to me to be a pitiable way for the person want- ing information to. adopt, though, with the Tory, it is quite zenaletent, fir he is not aupposed to know anything. He is supposed to believe and accept any statement made by those that are put in authority our u ...s_ , and thus we hid

him rushing into correspondence with Dukes, Earls, and 1 Rt. Hon. Gentlemen. The' Manchester Guardian," of July 27, 1880, contained 1 the following :—Mr. Gladstone, in reply to Mr. Bradlaugh, , said £B,OOO had been paid for Suez Canal qualification shares aa the 176,602 shares purchased by the late Govern- went did not qualify for directors. Why? Because the dividend coupons are detached from them until 1895. True it is the Egyptian Government agreed to pay five per cent. on the purchase money, but if we have to lend them the money to pay us it seems to me like borrowing 3s to pay back 2s again. Tbe "Manchester Courier" save Mr. Glad- stone said: It is stated that the present (1881) value of the shares is £7B. Ido not know if there is any legal provi- sion made as to whether these shares could be sold. Why? Because if the shares have never been in the market how can they Savo a market price: and if it was such a grand investment bow was it the Rotbchilds, lianderbilts, and Goechene, mined such a golden oppertunity ? Again, If the Government of this country are to be stock jobbers, let them go into it in the proper manner. But this is the great statesmanship of a bitter opponent of the cheap loaf; this guidance that has landed us in a war in Egypt and the Soudan; that has cost us millions of money, and, what is more, precious British lives. If this is the party who aie to 1 guide us in the future," Save us" is the cry of an ILLITERATE RADICAL.

div.head: DEPUTY MAYORALTY OF WARRINGTON..
div.p: THE DEPUTY MAYORALTY OF WARRINGTON..

Sir,—Your correspondent who wrote the peevish, dis- courteous, and uncalled for letter, under the nom de ',lime of" Boxer," which appeared in your issue of last Saturday is in error in supposing that the chair on the left of the Mayor, which I had the "presumption " to occupy at the last meeting of the Council, (and which trifling circum- stance seems so seriously to have disturbed his " bile ") is not the chair set apart for the "Deputy Mayor" at all. It lithe seat set apart for, and always used by, the" Ex- Mayor," (which designation I am well advised, is mine un- til the 9th Nov3mber next). True it is, that when the "Ex-Mayor" has been appointed "Deputy Mayor," (a Custom hitherto found convenient, and generally observed 'in Warrington and other places, perhaps more as an act ef Courtesy to the retiring Mayor, than anything else) be has been obliged to occupy the chair in question, seeing that be could not very conveniently resolve himself into two individealities at the same time. The appointment of " Deputy Mayor," rests with the Mayor alone, and not with the Council, therefore the Mayor 1,9 quite within his rights in not appointing ace Deputy," if, he shall so decide, as there is no legal obligation upon him to do so, the Coun- cil having full power to cope with any difficullilleo that his voluntary or enforced absence, might occasion. In conclusion, let me observe, that if yoer correspondent I. Bexer," (A very apt sobriquet I should think) had been influenced less by personal spleen, and more by a sincere and earnest desire to correct what appeared to him to be an irregularity. he would have taken the trouble to inform him- self of the bona flies, of his imaginary grievance, before rushing into print with a silly letter, in every line of which, in addition to its absurdity, there lurks a palpable secretion of venom, too feeble and puerile to sting, vet lacking not the quality (under the peculiar circumstances) to be offal- sive. Let me further remark, Mr. Editor, that while I don't wish to say anything unduly harsh of your correspondent, I nevertheless flud it difficult to believe he can be very familiar with the recognised amenities of even ordinary so- cial life, but, as a rule, I think "Boxers" are not usually credited with the possession of these qualities.—Yours obe- diently, Latchford, March 8, 1887.

div.head: J. HARRISON.
div.p: J. HARRISON.

THE ANTIQUITY OF THE EARTH AND THE ORIGIN OF MAN. Sir,—lt has been the fashion for some philosophical doe- trinairies to consider themselves much more advanced in intelligence than their fathers, and Mr. Peers is not the first by many who consid.r themselves superior to the philo• sophy which has sufficed for untold generations. He has heard two lectures and straightway comes to th 6 conclusion that the Mosaic account of the creation is wrong, because, forsooth, it does not square with the revelations of science. No future discoveries of science can ever invalidate the truths of religion, and religion being thus secure be would dispense with Moses. I should like to knew if he would substitute for the Mosaic anthropology, "The Vestiges of Creation." "The Origin of Species," and Spencer's " Rio• logy," because if be would, I would re.nind him that they occupy—even among scientists—a more debatable ground than ever Moses did. Men equally eminent AR scientific authorities are not agreed as to the teachings of the Great Stone Rook, and, Mr. Tuckwell notwithstanding. I would advise Mr. Peers not to be too sure "that one of the most recent of the life periods of the earth, comparatively a thing of yeeterday, must be calculated by more thousands than Moses ever dreamt of." Sir J. W. Dawson, president of the Royal Society. inlais recent book "The Story of the Earth and Man," gives it as his opinion that only 7,000 to 10,000 years have elapsed since the advent of man into the world. Be, of course, believes, as has been demonstrated beyond all doubt, that the earth is of immense antiquity, and Moses himself tells us nothing to the contrary. He tells us that prior to the creation the earth was without fore sod void, and that darkness covered the face of the earth—all of which is in accordance with the teachings of the Great Stone Book. _

_..,... .._.... This subject is a very wide one, and even to notice a few of its salient features would require far ampler space than Is afforded in the compaes of a letter. One feature, how- ever, I would like to notice—that as to the origin of man. Hugh Miller and Professor Dawson are utterly opposed to the hypotheses of evolution, and the gorillean origin of I ; man, and they strenuously affirm that it is without one I single shred of certain and conclusive evidence. Hugh I Miller, sem in "The Old Red Sandstone." "never yet was there a fancy so wild and extravagant, but there have been I men hold enough to dignify it with the name of philosophy, I and ingenious enough to find reasons for the propriety of i the name. Assuredly there 13 no lack of faith among in- fidel,; their vaulting credulity e'erleaps revelation, and falls on the other side." Sir J. W. Dawson says' This evolutionist doctrine is Itself one of the strangest phenomena lOU humanity. That in our day a system destitute of any shadow of proof,and supnorted merely by vague analogies and ' figures of speech,anff by the arbitrary and artificial coherence fed its own parts, should be accepted as a philosophy, and should find able adherents to string upon its thread of hypotheses our vast and weighty store of knowledge is surpassingly strange." When great masters of geology speak like this, is it not presumptions to talk of "belief go- ing to the dogs," and of the Bible having been tried and found wanting? I, at least, am not afraid that its teaching will be "shattered and condemned when the pupil comes to reason." One lesson—good for us all—we may learn from its sacred pages "to do justice and to love mercy, and to walk humbly before God," and if there are some things that we cannot understand the same is no less true in all the walks of science. Warrington, March let. JOHN CANDY. [We have not space for a controversy on this subject ; but we shall allow Mr. Peers, if he likes, to have a word in reply.—ED. Ex.] THE FREE LENDING LIBRARY MOVEMENT. Sir,—The bold and persistent manner in which you have advocated the Question of a Free Lending Library for War- rington has earned for you the thanks of large numbers of the most intelligent inhabitants of our town. The question is one in which I have all along taken a deep interest, and after taking every opportunity of finding out the opinion of the working people and others, by broaching the subject on all possible occasions, I can testify that a vast majority are in favour of our library being made free in the fullest sense of the term. I should like to state hare that very few of those I have spoken to seemed to be previously aware that they have been and are now paving a penny in the pound as a rate in support of the free library system, and that they cannot be `'tailed upon to pay more. Some few when this truth has ' dawned upon their minds have not been slows to cry ' " shame.," and express their sanee of injestice in terms the reverse of refined or flattering to the " big-wigs " who seek , to rule without reference to their wishes or power. The attitude assumed towards the matter by certain of our alder.nen and councillors, who have condescended to touch I It in response to the recent agitation, not because their ' tastes lead them in that direction, would be amusing, but that it indicates a pitiable amount of selfishness. Having all they require themselves, ibraries at home, or the means ' to pay the five shillings a year, and so have all the benefits of the Warrington Library at their own firesides, they for- get that large numbers are not en favourably circumstanced. One alderman—an inveterate quoter, and therefore we may Infer a great reader—Seems to treat us as so many spoiled children crying for the moon. He says, most complacently, the moon is too high up to be reached, and so we cant have it, and what is the use of hankering after it? He tells us a -Free Lending Library would ccet another £7,000, and, 1 as we cannot raise £l,OOO, we mast do without the Free Lending Library. This he evidently considers an easy and at the same time a dignified way of quietly getting rid of the question, which he would like to see dead and buried for this Jubilee year, and it may be for ever. Bet be is vastly mistaken if he thinks the people of Warrington will meekly accept his opinion and hold their made. They know that 1 this talk of £7,000 being required is pimply nonsense. You, sir, have shown that with a few hundred pounds a good start could be made. As you pointed out, we have not got to begin at the foundation, as there is already in existence a library of abott 20,000 volumes, purchased, I believe, chiefly by the ratepayers' money. Another gentleman last week ventured to doubt in public the existence of a strong feeling in the town in favour of a Free Lending Library. He thought If there were that we should have had evidence in the form of substantial sub- scriptions for the object by this time, after six months' talk- ing about it. He overlooked the fact that up to the time he spoke no money had been solicited by any properly consti- tuted authority for this or any other of the many pro- -sects in the air W celebrate the year of jubilee. This leads me to a. paint on which I wish to lay special emphasis. It is that the question is one which should be taken up and decided quite apart from, or at least indepen- dent of. Jubilee celebrations. It has an interest and im- portance infinitely transcending all these. It is a ratepayere' , question, and the coincidence of its being discussed in the I year when the Queen completes the fiftieth year of her i Ireign may or may not be favourable for its proper solution. But it must be faced and dealt with on its own merits, and 1 in view of its bearing on the welfare of the community, and ' if this be done the result is certain. Again, I have more than once been told that there is no need to make such a fuss; that we have already a good ' Library,and that it is practically free, the annual subscrip- tion being so small. I reply, it is unfair there should be any aubeeriptien at all required, and that the subscription

however small confines it to the few (who least need it), and binders the free use and fall usefulness of the library. I am a subscriber, and can perfectly well afford to pay the small amount; therefore cannot be charged with pleading merely for myself or from interested motives. It is rritter for regret, however, that the books taken out at the War- rington Library, Cr read within the building, are not at all in proportion to the volumes of excellent works it contains. I spent an hour in the Preston Free Library a fortnight ago, and took particular notice of the business going on there. The time was, I presume, the busiest; from eight to nine . in the evening. Two assistants were busily engaged ex- changing the books brought in by telegraph fads, working- men, shop girls and shop hobbledehoys, clerks, and others.' The scene was a busy one, full of life and activity, and yet ! marked by perfect order and system. Contrast this with; what is to be seen in Warrington on the evening of any day in the week. Only last Saturday evening I was in oar library for a considerable time making up a list from the catalogue. and during my stay the only other visitor was a nursemaid whose mistress had sent her with one book and to take back a certain other, which, however, did not happen to be in. Well. I thought, this is not as it should be. There are other aspects of the gne.stion I should liked to have touched upon, but I mast not extend my remarks at present as I have already made a somewhat large demand upon your space, not larger, however, than is warranted by the importance of the subject. With your leave I may take an opportunity of returning to it.—'Yours truly, ABRA CADABRA.
On Tuesday an inquest was held at South Tottenham on the body of a boy who died on Sunday afternoon. The jury found that death resulted from hydrophobia, ciused by the bite of a cat.

div.head: HOSPITAL*.
div.p: THE HOSPITAL*.

Dr. O'Keeffe presented a -11-s-CoTtTe ladies and gentlemen who had contributed papers, periodicals, and flowers to the Accident Hospital during the past year, and the cordial thanks of the Board were ordered to be conveyed to the donors. •

div.head: FL.nexcir.
div.p: FL.nexcir.

_ The minutes of the Finance Committee contained a letter from the Local Government Board stating that they had recommended the Public Works Loan Commissioners to advance £3,400 at 31 per cent., repayable by way of annu- ity over 37 years, and it was recommended that application be made for that amount for the Infectious Diseases Hospi- tal. item* amounting to £11,073 103 Id were recom- mended for Oayment.—The minutes were passed on the mo- tion of Mr. Handley. GENERAL PURPOSES. On the recommendation of this committee it was decided to petition In favour of the Leasehold Enfranchisement Bill. The surveyor had submitted a plan for the flagging of the front and sides of the new public offices estimated to cost £3OO. and instructions were given to advertise for tenders.

THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. Dr. O'Keefie proposed that application be made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow MOO for a caretaker's cottage at the. Infections Diseases Hospital.—Mr. Heyes seconded the motion, which was carried.

HOW STREETS ARE MADE. Mr. Midwood wished to call the attention of the Highway Committee to the manner in which streets were made. He understood that when the Board decided that cinder bottoms were to be put in that good rough clinker cinders were in- tended. In Wellington-street at the present time the material used for the foundation of that street was little better than soil ; and ' other streets were made much in the same way. It this method was to continue the Board would be required to remake the streets in a few years. It was of the greatest importance that good rough cinders should be used and not the streets merely taken up and put down again.—Mr. Carey said he was much obliged to Mr. Midwood for mentioning the snbject,which should have the immediate attention of the Highway Committee.-11r, Gas- kell doubted whether cinders were fit material for the bot- tom of street...-.. Mr. Carey stated that the committee and Surveyor were of opinion that cinders were a good bottom so long as they kept a good " skin " of macadam on the top of it. THE ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FEES.

In accordance with the notice he had given, Mr. Carey proposed that the fee of Is per day charged patients at the Accident Hospital be abolished. From information he had received he had reason to believe that this charge detracted considerably f-om the usefulness of the hospital. (Hear, hear.) The friends of injured workmen bad been known to object to allow them to go to the hospital en accoant of that payment, which in some cases formed a serious tax upon the resources of a family when the main bread winner had been made fticapab.e of earning wages. In going through the accounts for the past six years it was found that the average annual receipts in this manner was about £24, and that amount was all it would cost the ratepayers if the fees were abolished. lie thought it would be a grace- ful thing at the jubilee of her Majesty's reign, which they did not seem to be inclined to celebrate by any- thing generous, if they would be generous enough to remit these fees.—Mr.Gaskell seconded the proposition.— , Mr. ILeyes pointed out that about 12 months ago the Health Committee brought forward a resolution in similar terms, and there was only one vote recorded in favour of it, and that was his own. When the fees were abolished, there might be some patients who, Although not paupere, r,uight
AR
.CH

not be able to pay a medical man to attend to them, and Mr. Carey's proposition made no provisi.na for them. Now the proposition of the Health Committee did make an arrangement for this state of things, and for this reason he moved that the matter be referred to that committee.—Mr. Midwooi seconded—Mr. Carey said they had been wanting to bring the subject forward again.—Dr. O'Kewffe considered that the Health Committee was snubbed. He ex- pressed his sympathy with the abolition of the fee, but he nevertheless thought the Health Committee should have been consulted before this proposition was made Nineteen out a every twenty cases in the Accident Hos- pital were caused in the works of the town, and therefore the benefit would to a very great extent accrue te the manu- facturers. If a poor stranger got his leg broken by being run over by a cart, he could not be taken to the Accident Hospital, because he would not be able to pay Is per day, and the result would be that he would have to be conveyed to a Liverpool Hospital, which was supported by charitable persons. If they took away the Is per day they must do something else to support the hospital, and to keep down the rates. If the manufacturers would promise to contribute the deficiency in the charitable way other similar institu- tions were supportA be would be willing to abolish the fee. —Mr. Taylor said the abolition of the fee would make no difference to the manufacturers, as all the workmen were in a club.—The matter was referred to the Health Committee, this course being voted for by Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Sadler, Houghton, Heyes, Midwood, and Cook. Five members voted for Mr. Carey's proposal. There was no other business.

div.head: HOME RULE MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: HOME RULE MEETING AT WIDNES.

A public meeting was held in the Baths Assembly-room en Monday evening, under the auspices of the Widnes Division Liberal Association, for the purpose of hearing au address on "Mr. Gladstone's Borne Rule Scheme examined and defended" by Mr D. J. Sweeney, of Manchester. There was a good attendance. Mr. B. Carey occupied the chair, and he was supported by Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. McCambridge, Messrs. Sweeney, T. Shepherd, Little, B.A. (barrister of Liverpool), J. Taylor, T. Handley, J. Morrison, F. Reyes, F. Cave, F. Hartlaed, G. Ogg, T. Cosier, S. Sadler, W. Sadler, G. Rae. and H. B. Shores (secretary.) The Chairman, in a brief speech, said there were those who contended that Mr. Gladstone's plan was unworkable and unconstitutional, but he ventured to assert'that what- ever plan was introduced for the future government of Ire- land would not succeed unless it was in accordance with the will of the people of Ireland... (Applause.) .

. . Mr. Sweeney said Lord Salishui:i and is colleagues had I been for some months endeavouring to find is plan that would compete with Mr. Gladstone's in the government of Ireland, but their search had been utterly unsuccessful. One after another of Lord Salisbury's colleagues bad given up in despair their allotted share in the utterly impossible task of governing Ireland contrary to the wishes of her people, and though they might sympathies with Sir Michael Hicks Beach in the affection that had overtaken him, they might reasonably say that not 'merely had Sir Michael cataracts in his eves, but that the Government had cataracts, and was utterly unable to seo a way to govern the Irish people. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone proposed in his bill to establish a Parliament in Dahill) to which power was to be given to make laws far the local government of Ireland. He pro- posed to constitute that assembly in this way.: to add to the 103 members Ireland now elected to sit in the British House of Commons 103 other members who would be elected on the same franchise. To these 206 members were to be added 75 who were elected upon a property qualifica- tion franchise of £25, and the total number of 308 would be brought up ty the further addition of 25 of the peers who now sat in the Upper House at Westminster and as- sisted the English, Welsh, and Scotch peers in resisting the Commons of Great Britain. Mr. Gladstone proposed to give to that Parliament an Executive which would have the authority of enforcing the laws made in that assembly. He reserved for the control of the Impetial Par- liament all e,ueations of Imperial politics, and all questions relating to the government of the army and 1,1 the navy, and merely permitted the Parliament in Deblin to deal with matters purely Irish. According to his plan, the Irish Parliament would not be permitted to deal with the entire taxation of the country. The taxes recognised as Imperial would be levied by the Imperial ParliainenCand be collected in Ireland by agents of 'that Parliament. The , Irish Parliament would have the control of a small force of I police for the purpose of carrying out its behests. At pre- sent English authority was maintained in Ireland by about 25,000 soldiers and about 12,000 military police. Mr. Gladstone proposed to disband this police force, and to give to the Irish Parliament a force purely like the polic» force I In Lancashire, numbering 2,000 men, who would be charged with the maintenance of order. The first objection made to this scheme by Tories and Liberal Unionists was that it would effect the separation of Ireland from England. Under Home Rule English soldiers, under the control of the Imperial Parliament, would be quartered in Ireland—undoubtedly not in such numbers as at present, and bow dare the' Tories tell us that these soldiers, who had achieved such glorious feats upon all the battlefielde of Europe, would run helter ekelter before 2,000 Irish police I armed merely with blackthorn sticks. (Applause.) Such a charge the more closely it was examined by reasonable men, the more absurd it appeared. In reserving control ' over the army and navy, Mr. Gladstone bad given to the English people two strong guarantees for the maintenance of the union between Ireland and England. (Hear, hear.) Supposing the Irish people had e desire for separation, which be denied the existence of, England had the power of strangling it at its very inception by closing the Eng- lish markets to Irieh produce, and practically making that country bankrupt, and no country had ever been known to carry on a successful warfare against another without money in its treasury. (Applause.) As to banding over the Protestant minority to the "tender mercies of the , Catholic majority,', Mr. Sweeney pointed out that large I numbers of Protestant members had been returned to Par- liament by Ireland since the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, and with the one single exception of Daniel O'Connell, the Irish 1. tilers bad been ' Protestants. The Irish Catholic Corporations had appoint- ed to the Trost important office in their gift men who dif- fered from them in religion. In Cork and Dublin at the present time upwards of 50 per cent of the money spent in the payment of officials went into the pockets of Irish Pro- testants, while out of every hundred of the population 90 were Catholics. If there was any intolerance they must turn to the north to find it. In the city of Derry, where nearly half the population were Catholics, there With only one Catholic member in the Corporation, end there was not a single official in the pay of that large Corporation who happened to be a Catholic. Other instances of intolerance on the part of Orangemen were gived. The Irish Catholics were those who had been tolerant, and the Irish Catholics were those who might be relied upon in the future to be generous in their treatment of their Protestant and Presby- terian fellow countrymen, and he was delighted that the number of Protestant and Presbyterian Home Rulers was gradnally increasing, and that, it would soon be no longer possible for Mr. Chamberlain or anybody else to say that the Protestants of Ireland were opposed to Home Rule. (Applause) The motit absurd of all the ob- jections to Mr. Gladstone's Bill was that it would lead to the emigration into England of larger numbers of Irish labeurers than bad been accustomed to come every year. Strange tc say, since Mr. Gladstone made some improve- ment in the land tenure of Ireland, such an improvement as enabled the Irish tenants to participate to some extent in the ftuits of their own industry, the number of labourers who had come to England had been gradually on the de- crease, and tbe moment the Irish bad Home Rule given to them their attention would be directed to the development of their own country under a better system of land tenure. The Irish labourers would find plenty of means to exist in their own country without annually visiting England to snatch a few shillings from the English labourers in order that they nsight pay them over to the agents of the Irish landlord to be spent in vice and luxury in London. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Sweeney appealed to the audience no longer to support a Government which was too Tory even for Lord Randolph Churchill, and which dis- played its incompetence on every occasion; but at the next election to support a policy of justice and freedom to the Irish nation, and aid in cementing a union of heart and soul between the two countries that all the powers of earth er hell would be unable to rend asunder. (Loud applause.) Mr. T. Shepherd Little also addressed the meeting. After mentioning that he was a Protestant Irishman he entered into a scathing criticism of the position taken up by the more prominent Liberal Unionists, whOse policy he said was Toryism of the most pronounced type. He was confi- dent that in appealieg to the noblest side of the English nature, which had rejoiced in the growing freedom of every country in the world, the Irish would not plead in vain. (Applause.) On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Heyes, the hearty thanks of the meeting were tendered to the speakers. A vote of thanks was also accorded to the chairman who announced that on the 22nd inst. Mr. F. Cave would read a paper on the Irish question, to be followed by free discus- sion amongst the audience.

MB CLAIN BY A Docroa.—On Wednesday, at the County Court, his Honour Judge Thompson had before him the adjourned action of Dr. Casey against Mr. Andrew Jackson, manager for the Collins Green Colliery Company, for £l4 120 for surgical and medical attendance on four men who were seriously injured during the sinking of the Bold Colliery shaft, on the 19th May last. The case had been previously adjourned to see if an amicable settlement could not be come to. Mr. Thomas, of St. Helens, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, for the defendant.—Mr. Thomas said he was sorry to inform his Honour that a settlement had not been arranged. The plaintiff had offered to take £l2 in settlement of the debt and the costs, which was a very reasonable amount, but the defendant had only offered MO, which Dr. Casey could not accept, and he had, therefore, to ask for judgment. —After considerable discussion, his Honour held that he ' ought to take very much less, because when Mr. Jackson sent for a doctor he did not think he had authority to make the company liable, and did not think he would be liable himself. Mr. Davies thought three guineas for his attendance at the colliery on the day of the accident would he ample.—Elis Honour said he would give judgment for Mr. Jackson to pay that amount and costs to the plaintiff. —Mr. Thomas said this was a matter which affected the whole of the medical profession, and the St. Helens medi- cal gentlemen took great interest in it. He asked for leave to appeal. Ma Honour granted the application.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Bradford police have captured a gang of five camera, who have circulated a large number of false coins in York- shire. Three others are still at large. THB °Kok-rum—lt is stated that the Scotch members intend to raise a debate on the Naval estimates on the re- cent Naval expedition against the Crofters. A Blue Book of over 1,000 pages was issued to members of Parliament on Friday morning.containing minutes of the evidence taken by Lord Cowper's Irish Land Commission. In a letter received at Ambleside, Mr. Bright says:— " Regarding the proposed railway, the objections to the line seem to me to be absurd, and I trust the committee will be of my opinion!'

_ Mr. Randle Wilbraham, Higb Steward of Cengleton and sailor magietrate of the county of Chester, died at bia resi- dence, Rode Hall, Stoke-on-Trent, late on Thursday night. The deceased gentleman was born on New Year's Day, 1800.

Mmtus Dirarotesrnanox.—A large number of miners who are unemployed through the flooding of the shaft at Exhall Colliery paraded the adjacent villages on Friday, harnessed to a wagon, and soliciting hinds for their subsist- ence. Their novel appeal was liberally responded to. SNOWSTORM IN SCOTLANO.—Throughout Thursday night and Friday morning snow fell at Glasgow and in the West of Scotland. Trains between Edinburgh and Glas- gow were delayed, and in some parts the snowstorm is des- cribed as the severest for many years. Snow plouglui are being used. SHOCKING FATALITY.—The shocking death of a Welsh farmer was on Friday reported from Crosswood, Cardigan- shire. It appears that Mr. George Hughes. occupier of Wenallt Farm, was passing through the outbuildings with hie wife, when he came fn contact with, the driving rod of a turnip-pulper which was being worked by a water-wheel. He was immediately drawn into the machinery, and was dead before help was procured. A MaNcugerrne TRAGEDY.—The death occurred on Fri- day morning of Mrs. Gertrude Hyman, who was shot SO long ago as April last year by her husband Philip. Tie parties had lived separately, and the husband going to his wife's house in Shakespeare-street, Ardwick, shot her twice in the neck and head with a revolver. He afterwards blew his own brains out, and the jury in his case returned a ver- dict of suicide whilst insane. Mrs. Hyman has thus lin- gered almost a year after being wounded. WKILSH DISESTABLISHMENT.—A conference of Welshmen residing in London, nate held yesterday afternoon at Hol- born Town Hall. to consider the question of the disestablieh- ment of the Church of England in Wales. Mr. Richard M.P., preaided, and amongst those on the platform were a number of Welsh Members of Parliament, including Mr. oAborne Morgan. The Chairman explained that his motion in the House of Commons the other night was a test motion, to see how far their friends tbe dissentient Liberals would support them. The speakers included Mr. John Roberts, M.P., Mr. C. H. James, M.P , Mr. William Davies, M.P. A public fneeting was held in the evening, at which Sir Hussey Vivian presided.

div.head: LATE MR. BEECHER.
div.p: THE LATE MR. BEECHER.

A religious service was held on Thursday morning at Mr. Beecher's private residence, New York, after which the body woe removed to Plymouth Church, escorted by the 13th Regiment of the New York Volunteers, of which the deceased gentleman was the chaplain. The features, which were seen through the glass lid ef the coffin, bore a lifelike expression. Within a few hours twenty thousand people gazed for the last time on the face of the popular preacher. No crape, no emblems of mourning were displayed; but in their place was an unusual number and variety of wreaths, crosses, and other floral emblems.

div.head: RUNCORN BANKRUPTCIES.
div.p: RUNCORN BANKRUPTCIES.

Yesterday, at the Warrington County Court, Mr Henry Randle, draper, of 69, Bridge-street, Run- corn, appeared before the Registrar (Mr. Nicholson.) to undergo his public examination in bankruptcy. There were also present Mr. C. J. Dibb, the official rPceiverWr. A. B. Potter, his assistant, rind Air. Norris, of Liverpool, solicitor for Mr. Jackson, one of the creditors.—ln examination by Mr. Dibb, the debtor said a receiving order was made against him on his own petition. He filed his petition' because a previous meeting of creditors had failed to agree. He entered in business in March, 1880, having pre- viously been in Mr. Jackson's employ. He purchased the business from Mr. Jackson, for £1,960, and the fixtures for .6250. He borrowed the money to make these pnrchases. The bank, on Mr. George Hazle- burst's security, lent him £5OO, and his wife's bro- thers and sisters lent him another .£550. He had £lOO of his own capital; but he did not pay this to Mr. Jackson. The £1,050 which he borrowed, lie paid to Mr. Jackson, and the balance he agreed tp pay by quarterly instalments of .6.30 ss. The inter- est he was to pay upon the unpaid instalments was n per cent. ; he was to pay his wife's brothers and sisters 5 per cent., and the bank charged him 5 per cent. on the overdrawn account, in addition to commission. Mr. Jackson was the owner of the premises in which he carried on business, but he (the debtor) was not aware that by an agreement the rent was to be £221 per annum: that sum ,was never mentioned. He had always paid .£lOO per annurn.—The Official Receiver said the sum of £221 was in the agreement.—The Debtor said he had never beard that stint read over to him when the agreement was read over to him. He never intended the agreement to be of the nature of a bill of sale, and he would never have signed it if such' had beon intended. He was very much surprised when Mr. Jackson took possession in February, last, as Mr. Jackson had repeatedly told him he had absolutely no security. He would not have taken the business had not Mr, Jackson persuaded him to do so. He had intended to start in a small shop and spoke to Mr. Jackson about the latter stocking his shop, but Mr. Jackson ultimately suggested that hie should take over his business, and he pro- mitied to put on easy terms. He went through the valuation, but did not, check every item, but he Inow thought that he had paid .6750 too much in the valuation. He had always thought that he was giving too much for a portion of the stock.— The Official Receiver asked if that was so why did he give so much 2—The Debtor said he thought he was going to get rich in ten years. He instanced gloves in which he said he had in many cases sold at 3d and 6d per pair, for which he had paid 2s and Be per pair. By the stock he purchased he realised about £750 less than the valuation, and he attribu- ted his failure to bad trade, heavy rent, and having to overpay for his stock.—The Official Receiver said the debtor's deficiency, according to his own statement, was .62,200. He had given certain items which partly accounted for the deficiency, includ- ing X= overpaid for rent, .6750 overpaid for stock, and 45.R3 paid for interest. That made a total of £1,458, which left about .£762 un- accounted for. The debtor said he could not give any detailed account about that deficiency. He believed if his stock had been taken one week after he commenced business he would have been hopelessly insolvent.—ln reply to Mr. Norris, the debtor said, at the time he took the busi- ness from Mr. Jackson he complained about several of the items in the valuation. He believed that he could clear about .£2OO out 'of the business, and thought he might have made up any little over- charges theie might be.—Mr. George JackPon, one of the principal creditors, was then examined by the Official Receiver, after which the examination was adjourned to the 22nd April. Mr. Gregory was appointed trustee, with a committee of Inspection.
